Detailed physiology assessments in a relatively small number of well-characterized participants indicate wide interindividual variability in pharyngeal collapsibility and that ~70% have impairment in one or more non-anatomical endotype. In this study, we applied recently developed models that use standard clinical and polysomnography data to estimate OSA endotypes and oral appliance therapy response in a large clinical population. OSA endotypes and oral appliance therapy responses were estimated using standard sleep study outputs and clinical data (age and BMI) from > 6500 consecutive home-based diagnostic studies with an Apnoea/Hypopnea Index (AHI) > 5 events/h (Sleep Profiler PSG-Advanced Brain Monitoring). The proportion of participants who were estimated to have impairment in one or more OSA endotypes was calculated according to previously published physiological cutoffs. On average, participants (39% female) had moderately severe OSA (AHI = 28 ± 23 events/h [Mean ± SD]), were middle aged (49 ± 16 years) and obese (BMI = 31 ± 7 kg/m2). 29% were estimated to have only mild anatomical compromise. 23% had poor dilator muscles, 31% high loop gain and 29% had a low arousal threshold. 62% had severe ("bad") impairment in one or more non-anatomical endotypes. ~60% were predicted to respond to oral appliance therapy. These novel data highlight the heterogeneity of OSA in a large clinical OSA patient population and the feasibility for endotype-informed precision medicine for OSA via application of novel physiology-based algorithms using home sleep study recordings at scale.

title: Associations of Physical Activity With Mortality and Cardiovascular Diseases in Adults With Chronic Kidney Disease: A Community-Based Cohort Study.
text: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is linked to elevated risks of mortality and cardiovascular diseases (CVDs). This study aimed to investigate the dose-response associations of moderate-to-vigorous-intensity physical activity (MVPA) with all-cause mortality and CVD risk in adults with CKD. We included 3927 UK Biobank participants with CKD. Weekly MVPA duration was evaluated by wrist-worn accelerometers and a machine learning model. The primary outcomes were all-cause mortality and CVDs (heart failure, myocardial infarction, and stroke). Cox proportional hazards models and restricted cubic splines were used to assess the dose-response associations. CKD participants engaged in less MVPA than healthy controls. During a median follow-up of 7.92 years, 393 deaths and 445 CVDs occurred. Moderate-to-vigorous-intensity physical activity showed nonlinear associations with mortality and CVD risk. Mortality risk declined sharply up to 150 minutes per week MVPA and plateaued thereafter. Cardiovascular disease risk reached its lowest at approximately 300 minutes per week. Compared with <150 minutes per week, ≥150 minutes per week MVPA was associated with lower risks of mortality (hazard ratio = 0.64; 95% CI, 0.51-0.80) and CVDs (hazard ratio = 0.68; 95% CI, 0.55-0.83). Replacing sedentary behavior with MVPA for 10 min/d was associated with a significantly reduced mortality rate among less active CKD participants (hazard ratio = 0.70; 95% CI, 0.56-0.86). In adults with CKD, engaging in MVPA of ≥150 minutes per week was associated with significantly lower risks of mortality and CVDs. These findings underscore the value of physical activity promotion in CKD management.

title: Machine learning models for prioritizing referral for polysomnography: A comparison of quantum and conventional kernel approaches.
text: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a global health concern that demands accessible screening tools beyond resource-intensive polysomnography (PSG). However, PSG involves high medical costs and long waiting times. In this study, we developed quantum machine learning (ML; QML)-based OSA risk classification models using body profiles and compared their performances with conventional ML approaches. The predictors contributing most to the QSVM classification were also identified. We retrieved parameters of PSG and body profiles, including baseline characteristics and anthropometric metrics, from 4831 total participants. First, correlations among these parameters and comparisons across three OSA severity groups (normal-to-mild, moderate, and severe) were investigated. To establish classification models, a quantum-enhanced support vector machine (QSVM) and conventional algorithms, including logistic regression, k-nearest neighbors, naïve Bayes, support vector machine, random forest, and extreme gradient boosting were employed. Data were first divided into a training/validation dataset (80 %) and test dataset (20 %), with comparative analyses conducted to evaluate the classification performances of these ML approaches. Body profiles and PSG parameters significantly differed (p < 0.01) among the three OSA severity groups. Additionally, significant correlations (p < 0.01) were identified between body profile parameters and sleep-disordered breathing indices. On the test dataset, the QSVM achieved areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) of 76.60 % and 78.92 %, with accuracies of 72.97 % and 71.79 %, for the moderate-to-severe and severe classifications, respectively. The QSVM achieved discrimination comparable to that of most conventional models but did not show a consistent advantage. Its operating characteristics may support the prioritization of PSG scheduling.

title: Digital twin oncology and multi-omics-driven artificial intelligence models for personalized drug response prediction: A systematic survey of emerging computational paradigms and clinical implementation challenges.
text: The increasing complexity of tumor heterogeneity and variable therapeutic response has intensified the need for accurate personalized drug response prediction in oncology. Traditional trial-and-error chemotherapy strategies often result in suboptimal outcomes, toxicity, and delayed therapeutic adjustments. Rapid advances in multi-omics technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin modeling have significantly reshaped computational oncology research. This survey systematically reviews peer-reviewed research and review articles published from 2021 onward that investigate emerging computational paradigms integrating digital twins and multi-omics AI for drug response prediction. The foundational concepts in digital twin oncology, multi-omics profiling and AI-driven precision medicine are outlined initially. The existing approaches are categorized into four major paradigms such as omics-driven machine learning models, deep learning based multimodal architectures, mechanistic digital twin simulation frameworks and hybrid digital twin AI systems enabling adaptive therapy optimization. The multi-omics data integration strategies, including early, intermediate, late, network-based and graph/pathway-based fusion techniques. The survey synthesizes recent developments in drug sensitivity prediction, immunotherapy response modeling, tumor evolution forecasting and virtual clinical trials, while critically analyzing challenges related to data heterogeneity, interpretability, generalization, privacy, regulatory compliance and ethical considerations. Finally, future directions are highlighted such as real-time adaptive digital twins, federated learning, explainable AI and regulatory ready clinical deployment frameworks. Overall, this review provides a structured taxonomy, comparative analysis and research roadmap for advancing integrated digital twin and multi omics AI systems toward clinically actionable precision oncology.

title: Machine learning reveals pre-treatment deficit accumulation as a predictor of persistent cancer-related fatigue: The Thinking and Living with Cancer longitudinal cohort study.
text: Cancer-related fatigue is a long-term, distressing symptom among older survivors. However, predictors of fatigue are not well defined. We used machine learning to identify pre-treatment factors that predict persistent fatigue among older breast cancer survivors. Participants were women ages ≥60 with non-metastatic breast cancer enrolled pre-systemic treatment (n = 543) and age, race, and site-matched controls without a cancer history (n = 496). Fatigue was assessed using the Functional Assessment of Chronic Illness Therapy-Fatigue (FACIT-F) fatigue subscale at baseline, one year, and two years; persistent fatigue was defined as ≤34 points at year one and/or two. Baseline variables included demographics, medical history, lifestyle habits, symptoms, a 46-item deficit accumulation index (DAI; an indicator of frailty) score, and cancer and treatment details (survivors only), yielding 90 variables for survivors and 82 for controls. Logistic regression with Lasso variable selection, Stochastic Gradient Boosting, Random Forest, and Boruta machine learning models were applied to assess factors that predicted persistent fatigue. Participants were 68.4 ± 6.1 years; 14.4% of survivors and 8.1% of controls reported persistent fatigue (p = 0.002). Model performance was strong across algorithms (corrected AUROC range: 0.74-0.83). For all participants, predictors of persistent fatigue included higher baseline fatigue, as measured using the FACIT-F total score or FACIT-F fatigue subscale score. Notably, higher pre-treatment DAI score was a strong predictor among survivors across all models (p < 0.001) but was selected by only one model for controls. Greater pre-treatment DAI score was predictive of persistent fatigue in older breast cancer survivors. Thus, a higher DAI score may be a useful clinical indicator of fatigue risk, helping target intervention efforts for these patients. gov identifier:NCT03451383.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Sentiment Analysis in Pregnancy-Related Weight Discussions on Reddit: Human Performance-Aligned Comparative Evaluation Study.
text: Pregnancy-related weight gain is both physiologically complex and socially charged, and online discussions often combine clinical information with implicit emotional distress. Although automated sentiment analysis could support research on pregnancy-related discourse, model performance in this context remains inadequately characterized relative to expert human judgment. This study aimed to benchmark contemporary sentiment classification models on pregnancy-related weight discussions, with emphasis on agreement with expert consensus, interpretive ambiguity, task adaptation, and deployment across posts and comments. We curated 15,619 Reddit posts and comments using a large language model (LLM)-guided keyword expansion strategy and established an adjudicated consensus reference set of 200 posts. We evaluated 10 models on a fixed held-out test set (N=150) using aligned text inputs, weighted performance metrics, and 1000-resample bootstrap CIs. RoBERTa (Robustly Optimized Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers Approach) and BERTweet (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers for Tweets) were additionally evaluated in a 5-fold fine-tuning sensitivity analysis. Gemini-3-Flash (Google DeepMind [Google LLC]) and Generative Pretrained Transformer (GPT)-OSS (OpenAI) were then applied to 400 unlabeled posts and 15,019 comments with intermodel agreement assessment. To expand expert-labeled coverage, a separate 106-post annotation extension was used for secondary evaluation of the 2 models carried forward to post-level corpus inference, and cross-source recoverability of the API-derived retrieval was assessed using Arctic Shift (Arthur Heitmann). The 2 primary experts (FAK and BMW) achieved 59.0% preadjudication agreement (Cohen κ=0.344). In the fixed held-out comparison, Gemini-3-Flash had the numerically highest weighted F1-score of 0.662 (κ=0.478), followed by GPT-OSS (F1-score=0.645; κ=0.436), with overlapping CIs across leading models. Under the harmonized direct-argmax decision rule with minimally processed text, BERTweet achieved an F1-score of 0.623 (κ=0.369), and RoBERTa achieved an F1-score of 0.605 (κ=0.339). In the separate fine-tuning sensitivity analysis, the mean cross-validated F1-score was 0.708 (SD 0.087) for RoBERTa and 0.616 (SD 0.079) for BERTweet. Among Gemini-3-Flash errors, 55.8% (29/52) occurred in posts on which the 2 primary experts disagreed. In the 106-post annotation extension, primary-expert agreement was 64.2% (68/106; κ=0.367); Gemini-3-Flash and GPT-OSS achieved weighted F1-score values of 0.633 and 0.680, respectively, and both identified 56 of 58 expert-negative posts in an exploratory human-review prioritization analysis. All 714 API-retrieved post IDs were independently recoverable through Arctic Shift. Intermodel agreement was 92.3% for posts (κ=0.797; n=400 valid pairs) and 46.3% for comments (κ=0.102; n=1500). No single model architecture was uniformly superior, and performance depended on the adaptation regime, annotation ambiguity, and discourse type. These findings define important boundary conditions for sentiment analysis of naturalistic maternal-health discourse: broad polarity classification can support corpus prioritization and hypothesis generation but is insufficient as a stand-alone measure of patient experience.

title: Interpretable Recalibration of a Sequential Organ Failure Assessment-Derived Score Using Machine Learning-Guided Optimization: Multicenter Cohort Study.
text: The Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score is central to risk stratification in intensive care units (ICUs), but its thresholds and 0- to 4-point increments were set by expert consensus in 1996 and never reestimated from outcome data. Machine learning models discriminate better while discarding the additive, point-based structure that makes SOFA auditable at the bedside, and methods for updating a legacy score rather than replacing it remain scarce. This study aimed to develop and internally validate a data-driven recalibration of a SOFA-derived score that learns thresholds and integer weights from outcome data while preserving an additive, interpretable point-based structure and to test whether it improves discrimination for ICU mortality over a prespecified SOFA-derived reference score. We conducted a retrospective multicenter cohort study using the eICU Collaborative Research Database (208 US hospitals, 2014-2015). We analyzed 14,848 adult first ICU admissions with complete day 1 SOFA-related measurements; 133,684 (90%) of 148,532 encounters with outcome data were excluded because of at least 1 missing determination. As vasoactive dose units could not be harmonized and urine output was largely unavailable, a prespecified SOFA-derived reference score served as the comparator. The framework couples supervised discretization (univariate decision trees and interval number chosen by a penalized validation criterion) with constrained integer-weight optimization under monotonicity, integrality, and scale-anchoring constraints, plus logistic calibration. Performance was estimated from pooled out-of-fold predictions of 10-fold nested cross-validation grouped by hospital, with bootstrap CIs; final thresholds and weights were refit on the full cohort and contributed no performance estimate. ICU mortality was 17.03% (2529/14,848). The recalibrated score achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.811 (95% CI 0.800-0.819) versus 0.751 (95% CI 0.740-0.761) for the reference score (paired difference 0.059, 95% CI 0.053-0.067), and an area under the precision-recall curve of 0.495 (95% CI 0.477-0.515) versus 0.393 (95% CI 0.377-0.411; paired difference 0.102, 95% CI 0.087-0.116). Improvement was consistent across all 10 hospital-grouped folds and length-of-stay strata. After unweighted logistic recalibration, global calibration was adequate; the Brier score was lower (0.112 vs 0.123), whereas other calibration-error measures were higher. Discrimination approached unconstrained XGBoost (Extreme Gradient Boosting; AUROC 0.818) and exceeded penalized logistic regression (AUROC 0.775) fitted on the same folds. The advantage persisted in all 1000 resampling replications and in a prespecified sensitivity analysis expanding the cohort to 61,469 encounters (median paired AUROC difference 0.037). Data-driven recalibration under explicit structural constraints can update the cutpoints and integer weights of an established clinical score without abandoning its additive, bedside-computable form and should transfer to other legacy instruments. The recalibrated score is a mortality risk model on its own 0-71 scale; an open-source calculator is provided, and external and prospective validation is required before clinical use.

title: Hallucinated Evidence and Real-World Risk-Physicians' Intent to Act on AI-Generated Abstracts in Emergency Medicine and Trauma Surgery: Cross-Sectional, Vignette-Based Diagnostic Accuracy Study.
text: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in academic writing and can generate linguistically polished but factually incorrect scientific content. Such misinformation may distort evidence appraisal and, if translated into clinical practice, compromise patient care. This study aimed to estimate physicians' likelihood of misperceiving false information embedded in LLM-generated abstracts as true and reporting an intent to use that information in future practice. We also explored which features were associated with perceived credibility and intended clinical action. We conducted a cross-sectional, vignette-based survey of physicians working in emergency medicine and trauma surgery across 4 hospitals in Germany. Each participant assessed 4 abstracts generated using GPT-5 Thinking mode, of which 2 contained intentionally false claims supported by plausible explanations and 2 contained accurate claims. The primary outcome was the proportion of physicians reporting an intent to use or act on recommendations contained in abstracts with false claims. Secondary outcomes included perceived accuracy, rejection of accurate claims, and ratings of precision, structure, and grammar. Twenty physicians provided 80 ratings of 4 abstracts. Overall, physicians reported that they would act on 68% (54/80) of abstracts. Using abstract truth status as the reference, the decision to act had a sensitivity of 78% (31/40), specificity of 43% (17/40), positive predictive value of 57% (31/54), and negative predictive value of 65% (17/26). The positive likelihood ratio was 1.35 (95% CI 0.98-1.85), the negative likelihood ratio was 0.53 (95% CI 0.27-1.04), and the diagnostic odds ratio was 2.55 (95% CI 0.96-6.73). True and false abstracts received similar ratings for perceived accuracy (mean 3.15, SD 0.89 vs mean 2.88, SD 1.04; P=.21), precision (mean 3.15, SD 0.89 vs mean 2.93, SD 1.00; P=.29), structure (mean 3.23, SD 0.77 vs mean 3.20, SD 0.88; P=.89), and grammar (mean 3.40, SD 0.59 vs mean 3.43, SD 0.68; P=.86). Abstracts that physicians intended to act on were rated substantially higher for perceived accuracy, precision, and structure than those they would not act on (all P<.001), whereas grammar ratings did not differ (P=.80). Physicians frequently reported an intent to act on LLM-generated abstracts containing false claims, and true and false abstracts were not reliably distinguished on perceived quality measures. Perceived accuracy, precision, and structure were strongly associated with intended action, whereas grammar was not. These findings highlight the risk that persuasive scientific presentation may increase the credibility and potential clinical influence of fabricated or inaccurate AI-generated evidence.

title: Large Language Model-Assisted Discharge Instructions for Diabetic Kidney Disease: Comparative Evaluation Study.
text: Discharge instructions are an important component of the transition from hospital to home for patients with diabetic kidney disease (DKD), whose care often involves multiple comorbidities, medications, and stage-specific management needs. However, producing complete, accurate, clear, and personalized instructions can be challenging for junior physicians. This study aimed to evaluate whether large language model (LLM) assistance improves the quality of DKD discharge instructions produced by junior physicians and whether its benefits vary according to chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage. The study included 101 hospitalized patients with DKD. Discharge instructions for each patient were initially drafted by a group of junior residents (resident group); subsequently, another group of residents at the same level, with the assistance of DeepSeek-V3.2 (AI-assisted group), generated a separate set of discharge instructions for the same 101 patients, resulting in a total of 202 documents. Four clinical experts, including 2 nephrologists and 2 endocrinologists, independently scored both versions of the discharge instructions using a 5-point Likert scale across 5 dimensions: completeness, accuracy, safety, clarity, and personalization. Interrater reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC). Interrater reliability was excellent in both the resident group (ICC=0.817, 95% CI 0.763-0.864; P<.001) and the AI-assisted group (ICC=0.860, 95% CI 0.816-0.897; P<.001). Compared with resident-only instructions, AI-assisted instructions received significantly higher scores across 5 evaluation dimensions and the overall evaluation (all Bonferroni-adjusted P<.001), with large effect sizes (r=0.741-0.927). In the resident-only group, CKD stage was negatively correlated with accuracy, safety, clarity, and overall quality (Spearman ρ=-0.33 to -0.37; all P<.001), whereas no significant correlations were observed for most dimensions in the AI-assisted group (|ρ|<0.15; P>.05). The proportion of cases achieving a ≥1-point improvement in overall quality was 99% (100/101; 95% CI 94.6%-100.0%). LLM assistance improved the completeness, clarity, and personalization of DKD discharge instructions generated by junior physicians, with advantages greatest in complex cases. A human-AI collaborative model is a promising approach to reduce documentation burden.

title: MAIT cells exacerbate early liver fibrosis by downsizing the intrahepatic regulatory T cell compartment.
text: Mucosa-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells have been paradoxically implicated in tissue repair and fibrosis. However, when and how they modulate fibrogenesis in distinct tissue environments remain unclear. Using the carbon tetrachloride model of liver injury in major histocompatibility complex-related protein 1 (MR1)- and MAIT cell-sufficient and -deficient mice, we identify MAIT cells as early drivers of fibrogenesis. MAIT cells exacerbated hepatocellular injury, myofibroblast activation, and matrix deposition during fibrosis initiation, coinciding with rapid polarization toward a MAIT17 phenotype and induction of a profibrotic transcriptional program. Despite acquiring an exhaustion-associated phenotype, MAIT cells retained their effector functions. Mechanistically, MAIT cells limited hepatic regulatory T (Treg) cell accumulation, accompanied by reduced Ki-67 and CXCR3 levels in the latter population. Furthermore, in vivo Treg cell inactivation abrogated MAIT cell-dependent differences in fibrosis severity. Together, these findings identify MAIT cells as early orchestrators of fibrogenesis and reveal a previously unappreciated MAIT-Treg axis that can be therapeutically targeted in the early stages of fibrotic diseases.

title: Machine learning approaches for the identification of real-world predictors of mepolizumab response.
text: Mepolizumab improves control and reduces clinically significant exacerbations in severe asthma patients. Further research is needed to understand factors influencing patient response. Identify predictors of response to mepolizumab using machine learning techniques. Thirty clinically relevant features from the REALITI-A dataset were analyzed. Response to mepolizumab was defined as change in clinically significant exacerbations at Year 1 post-exposure, being free from clinically significant exacerbations at Year 1, and being free from clinically significant exacerbations at both Year 1 and Year 2 post-exposure for primary, secondary, and exploratory analyses, respectively. Linear/logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost models were tested. The best-performing model based on R2 or classification accuracy was used for feature selection. A SHapley Additive exPlanations post-hoc analysis was conducted. The primary and secondary analyses included 685 patients; the exploratory analysis included 529 patients. Using XGBoost for the primary analysis, higher pre-exposure clinically significant exacerbations rate, lower body mass index, total immunoglobulin E, lower baseline activity impairment, and lower baseline Asthma Control Questionnaire-5 score were top predictors. For the secondary analysis, the random forest model identified lower pre-exposure clinically significant exacerbations rate, residency outside the United Kingdom, and lower baseline Asthma Control Questionnaire-5 score, body mass index, and baseline activity impairment as top predictors. For the exploratory analysis, XGBoost identified residency outside the United Kingdom, and lower pre-exposure clinically significant exacerbations rate, baseline Asthma Control Questionnaire-5 score, eosinophil levels, and body mass index as top predictors. Machine learning models identified key predictors of response to mepolizumab, which could guide clinical decision-making and improve patient outcomes in severe asthma patients.

title: Application of artificial intelligence in acute myocardial infarction: A bibliometric analysis from 2016 to 2025.
text: Growing interest suggests that the broad application of artificial intelligence (AI) in acute myocardial infarction (AMI) has advanced diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment. AI methods applied to AMI research have recently yielded significant predictive outcomes. However, few studies have systematically analyzed this field using bibliometric approaches. We employ CiteSpace to examine the visual relationships of publications, identify key research trends and hotspots, and stimulate broader participation in AI-AMI studies. Data for this bibliometric analysis were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection. A systematic search strategy was developed using Medical Subject Headings to identify publications pertaining to AI in AMI from January 2016 to December 2025. The initial query returned 2089 records, which were subsequently refined through manual screening and algorithmic deduplication, yielding a final corpus of 2088 eligible publications. Bibliometric analyses were performed using CiteSpace (version 6.2.R6) with the following configuration: annual time slices of 1 year, a selection threshold of the top 25 most frequent items per slice (Top N = 25), and network pruning via the Pathfinder algorithm applied to both sliced and merged networks. Multidimensional analyses were conducted across six node types - country/region, institution, author, cited author, cited journal, and keyword - employing co-occurrence mapping, co-citation analysis, cluster detection, and burst term identification. These approaches collectively delineated the intellectual landscape, collaborative architectures, and thematic evolution characterizing the AI-AMI research domain. We analyzed publications, citations, and networks. Post-2016, publications surged from 24 (2016) to 517 (2025) with dramatically increasing citations. Global collaboration centered on the China (705 publications), USA (553 publications), and India (195 publications), with Harvard-linked institutions forming the dominant cluster (e.g., Harvard University: 100 publications, centrality = 0.12). Author networks identified key bridges Saba, Luca (13 publications, centrality = 0.05) and Pontone, Gianluca (centrality = 0.06), contrasting with high-output but low-centrality authors like Acharya, U Rajendra (21 publications). High-centrality cited authors (e.g., ACHARYA UR: centrality = 0.09) were pivotal nexuses. Journal analysis showed CIRCULATION (1375 cites) and J AM COLL CARDIOL (1120 cites) as citation leaders. Keywords revealed evolving focus: prevalent terms ("myocardial infarction": 698 freq., "machine learning": 603 freq.) were highly productive, whereas central terms ("prediction": centrality = 0.36, "acute myocardial infarction": centrality = 0.24) bridged domains. Keywords bursts shifted from computational themes pre-2020 (e.g., "neural network," strength = 8.31) to the practical application of AI post-2020 (e.g., "system," strength = 5.43 and "prevalence," strength = 4.61). AI-AMI research exhibits globally distributed multilevel collaboration structures anchored by major nations/institutions and critical author bridges. Knowledge dissemination hinges on domain-bridging journals like CIRCULATION. Thematic emphasis has evolved from computational techniques towards clinical applications, interconnected by high-centrality concepts.

title: ChatGPT-related research in medical education: A dual-database bibliometric review and science-mapping analysis, 2023 to 2026.
text: The medical-education literature on ChatGPT has grown rapidly since 2023, but bibliometric patterns vary with database coverage, indexing fields, and the boundary used to define educational relevance. We examined publication growth, collaboration, and thematic development and assessed whether the leading patterns were stable under a stricter topic definition. Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) and PubMed were searched on September 5, 2026; the PubMed publication-date filter extended through September 4, 2026. WoSCC supported citation- and Author Keyword-based science mapping, whereas PubMed provided a complementary Medical Subject Headings-based view. The expanded corpora contained 665 WoSCC and 1106 PubMed records, with strict topic-specific subsets of 532 and 898 records, respectively. Bibliometrix/R, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, and Microsoft Excel were used for descriptive bibliometrics, collaboration networks, thematic mapping, multiple correspondence analysis, keyword co-occurrence, Trend Topics, burst detection, and journal mapping. Data from 2026 were treated as partial-year observations. WoSCC publication output increased from 66 records in 2023 to 169 in 2024 and 242 in 2025; 188 records were indexed during the partial 2026 period. The United States had the largest corresponding-author output, and Sichuan University was the leading displayed affiliation. The keyword structure centered on medical education, ChatGPT, artificial intelligence, and large language models. CiteSpace identified 9 keyword clusters, including medical education, large language models, medical students, generative artificial intelligence, prompt engineering, clinical decision-making, and patient education. Recently emerging terms included DeepSeek, clinical reasoning, and anatomy education. Author Keyword rankings were highly concordant between the expanded and strict WoSCC datasets (Spearman ρ = 0.973, P < .001). ChatGPT-related medical-education research expanded substantially after 2023 and diversified across assessment, clinical reasoning, educational applications, and broader LLM-related themes. The leading WoSCC keyword structure remained stable under the stricter topic definition. WoSCC and PubMed captured different bibliographic features and are best interpreted as complementary sources.

title: Predictive model for acute kidney injury in critical patients with pulmonary embolism based on machine learning: A multicenter clinical study.
text: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is recognized as an acute, critical cardiovascular condition, and acute kidney injury (AKI) is frequently observed as a complication in this clinical context. Currently, no predictive tools are available to accurately assess AKI risk in critical patients with PE. A predictive model was developed in this study to estimate AKI risk in critical PE. Data obtained from Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV were utilized for the development of training and internal validation sets, while data derived from Emergency Intensive Care Unit Collaborative Research Database were employed for external validation. Eight machine learning models were developed through least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression and multivariate logistic analysis, and a web-based calculator was subsequently deployed. Model performance was evaluated by receiver operating characteristic curve analysis, calibration curve assessment, and decision curve analysis to determine discrimination, calibration accuracy, and clinical utility. Feature importance within the optimal performing models was quantified through Shapley Additive eXplanation analysis. Incremental predictive value relative to the pulmonary embolism severity index score was evaluated via net reclassification improvement and integrated discrimination improvement. A total of 2187 and 2183 patients diagnosed with critical PE were enrolled by 2 centers. In the training set, 1725 (78.88%) patients had AKI, whereas 1185 (54.28%) patients had AKI in the validation set. Hypertension, heart failure, pneumonia, sepsis, ventilation, respiratory rate, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, partial pressure of oxygen, lactate, and Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score were ultimately identified as risk factors for AKI in critical PE. The extreme gradient boosting model demonstrated the most stable discrimination, calibration, and clinical benefit across training (area under curve [AUC] = 0.825), internal validation (AUC = 0.771), and external validation (AUC = 0.757) sets. Shapley Additive eXplanation analysis of the optimal model revealed that Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and partial pressure of oxygen contributed substantially to AKI risk. Relative to the pulmonary embolism severity index model, the proposed model exhibited superior performance in predicting AKI. A machine learning prediction model that integrates clinical indicators with disease activity scores was constructed and externally validated to estimate the risk of AKI in critical PE. A web-based calculator was subsequently developed to enable clinicians to identify high-risk cohorts and furnish evidence-based guidance for early intervention and individualized management.

title: Machine learning-guided discovery and preliminary biological evaluation of novel GSK-3β inhibitory scaffolds with anti-inflammatory potential.
text: Glycogen synthase kinase-3β (GSK-3β) is a multifunctional serine/threonine kinase implicated in neurodegeneration, cancer, metabolic disorders, and inflammatory diseases. The discovery of structurally novel GSK-3β inhibitors remains important for developing new chemical probes and therapeutic starting points. In this study, we established a machine learning-assisted computational screening workflow for the identification of potential GSK-3β inhibitors. A Random Forest (RF) classification model was trained using a curated dataset of reported GSK-3β-related compounds collected from 2016 to 2024. The optimized RF model showed good predictive performance, with an accuracy of 0.89 and an AUC-ROC of 0.91 ± 0.02, supporting its use as an initial prioritization tool for virtual screening. The trained classifier was applied to the Asinex compound library, and prioritized compounds were further evaluated through physicochemical and ADMET filtering, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations. This integrated workflow led to the selection of two representative candidates, RF03 and RF05, for experimental validation. In vitro enzymatic assays confirmed moderate GSK-3β inhibitory activity, with IC₅₀ values of 85.04 µM for RF03 and 58.73 µM for RF05. Among them, RF05, which contains a non-classical and sterically hindered aromatic ester scaffold, also reduced the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF-α and IL-6, while maintaining low cytotoxicity under the tested conditions. Overall, this study demonstrates the feasibility of combining machine learning-based prioritization with structure-based modeling and biological evaluation to identify previously underexplored GSK-3β inhibitory scaffolds. Although RF05 requires further optimization to improve potency, selectivity, and pharmacological properties, it provides a useful starting point for the development of next-generation GSK-3β-targeted anti-inflammatory agents.

title: Diagnostic Value in Discarded Reads: Re-evaluating Multi-Mapping cfDNA Fragmentomics and GC Bias in Early-Stage Cancer.
text: BackgroundLow-coverage plasma cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing is an inexpensive substrate for cancer detection. Standard pipelines discard fragments with low mapping quality, which originate mostly from repetitive DNA, although pericentromeric satellite repeats are frequently hypomethylated in cancer. We asked whether the fraction of multi-mapping cfDNA fragments differs between early-stage cancer and matched healthy controls, and how it compares with conventional fragmentomic features under strict control of technical factors. MethodsWe analysed public plasma cfDNA whole-genome sequencing from 25 patients with stage I-III breast cancer and 25 healthy controls matched 1:1 for age, sex, smoking and alcohol use, each pair processed in the same library and sequencing batch, and from 8 early-stage hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cases with 8 matched controls. For every sample we computed the fraction of autosomal fragments with MAPQ < 30 and the share of these fragments located in centromeric and heterochromatic cytobands, and related them to stage, grade and copy-number deviation as proxies of tumour burden. Classifiers were evaluated by leave-one-pair-out cross-validation in breast cancer and, trained on breast cancer only, applied unchanged to HCC. Robustness to GC content and sequencing depth was tested by within-fold residualisation and by fragment-level GC weighting. Conventional fragmentomic features (fragment length, end motifs, copy number, DELFI-like profiles and window features at transcription start sites) were evaluated under four GC-handling analyses. ResultsThe multi-mapping fraction was higher in breast cancer than in matched controls (median 5.38 % vs 5.19 %; higher in 19/25 pairs; paired p = 0.0006; cross-validated AUC 0.81, 95% CI 0.67-0.94), in stage I (9/10 pairs), stage II (7/10) and stage III (3/5) disease and in every sequencing batch. The excess was concentrated in centromeric and heterochromatic bands, whose share of multi-mapping fragments rose from 22.0 % to 23.4 % (19/25 pairs; p = 0.004). Both signals persisted after within-fold adjustment for GC content and/or depth (AUC 0.64-0.76 for the multi-mapping fraction, 0.71-0.76 for the heterochromatic share) and under fragment-level GC weighting (18/25 pairs; p = 0.003). The multi-mapping difference was largest in stage I and decreased with stage (Spearman {rho} = -0.42, p = 0.04), and neither feature was associated with grade or copy-number deviation. In public tissue methylomes, satellites were hypomethylated in breast tumours to a similar extent as other late-replicating DNA, but the bin-level association between tumour hypomethylation and the cfDNA excess was weak and was explained by GC content. In HCC, the pre-specified endpoint, the breast-trained multi-mapping model, was not met (AUC 0.73; 5/8 pairs; sign test p = 0.36). In an exploratory analysis that was not pre-specified, the heterochromatic share was higher in 7/8 HCC pairs (p = 0.016; locked AUC 0.86, 95 % CI 0.62-1.00); across all 33 pairs, including the discovery pairs, it was higher in the cancer case in 26 (post hoc sign test p = 0.0007). In contrast, conventional fragmentomic features reached AUC 0.71 (breast) and 0.77 (HCC) only without fragment-level GC control; they tracked the per-sample coverage-GC dependence and fell to chance under each of three GC-controlled analyses, including one that preserves promoter-specific signal. ConclusionsMulti-mapping cfDNA fragments, which are routinely discarded, differed between early-stage breast cancer and batch-matched controls, largely independently of GC content and sequencing depth, with an excess in centromeric and heterochromatic DNA. The signal did not scale with stage, its biological origin is unproven, and a read-quality contribution cannot be excluded from fragment files. It is a candidate marker that requires confirmation in larger cohorts with raw reads and tumour-fraction estimates.

title: ShortKit-ML: an open toolkit for measuring shortcut potential in medical imaging embeddings
text: Background and ObjectiveA classifier trained on frozen embeddings can take a shortcut through a sensitive attribute only if the embedding carries information about it beyond what the task label explains: its shortcut potential. We asked whether this can be measured on the embedding alone with a known false positive rate, and whether it predicts how strongly a classifier trained on confounded data relies on the attribute. MethodsShortKit-ML tests whether an embedding E and a sensitive attribute A are dependent given a task label Y. The primary test is a conditional probe: a logistic regression that predicts A from E and Y, scored by out-of-fold AUROC and calibrated by permuting A within levels of Y, between patients. Five secondary detectors share this null. We audited sex, age and race for seven frozen encoders on CheXpert and four on MIMIC-CXR, and trained heads on confounded CheXpert splits. ResultsUnder the null the probe rejected in 0.02 of synthetic data sets. With A and Y strongly correlated, an unconditional probe rejected in 0.95 and the conditional probe in 0.03. No detector found signals that leave group means unchanged, unlike probes on squared or product features under the same null. The probe found attribute information in 21 of 21 CheXpert and 12 of 12 MIMIC-CXR cells. Across 42 CheXpert cells the probe score correlated with the true positive rate gap of a confounded head (Spearman 0.60, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.80 resampling encoders), 0.74 within sex and not significantly within age. Three embedding-level mitigations changed the gap by at most 0.01 relative to their controls. Refitting the head on a group-balanced subset closed it. A planted image marker was found in all 10 seeds. ConclusionsOne calibrated linear test measures shortcut potential on a frozen embedding, and on CheXpert its score correlated with how strongly a confounded logistic head relied on the attribute, clearly for sex. It does not show that a given head uses the attribute, and lowering the score did not remove reliance, so the head itself must be tested as well. Code is at https://github.com/criticaldata/ShortKit-ML.

title: Dense Breast Tissue Segmentation under Limited Annotation: Comparing CNNs, Transformers, Self-Supervision, and Prompting
text: Dense breast tissue reduces the sensitivity of mammographic screening and is an important risk factor for breast cancer, making accurate dense-tissue segmentation particularly important when expert pixel-level annotations are limited. We empirically study dense breast tissue segmentation under limited pixel-level supervision using a small expert-annotated dataset (596 images) together with an in-domain unlabeled mammography dataset (20,000 images). We compare classical pixel-level segmentation methods, CNN and U-Net encoder-decoder models, transformer-based models, self-supervised pre-training, fine-tuning strategies, loss functions, and prompt-based MedSAM variants under a unified evaluation protocol. CNN-based models achieve the best standalone segmentation performance while providing the most favorable balance between accuracy and computational cost. In contrast, the adaptive fuzzy c-means + SVM baseline and transformer-based models perform worse in this low-label setting. Our analysis of prompt-based MedSAM further shows that SAM-style models are highly sensitive to prompt quality. Box and breast-region prompts lead to poor performance, whereas CNN-generated dense prompts substantially improve MedSAM performance. However, even with mask-decoder fine-tuning, CNN-prompted MedSAM does not outperform the best standalone CNN model, suggesting that current SAM-style models require stronger prompts or adaptation beyond the mask decoder for diffuse breast-density segmentation. Additionally, a density-calibrated hybrid loss primarily improves percentdensity calibration by reducing the test MAE from 14.8 to 11.8 percentage points. Our computational cost analysis indicates that many generic self-supervised learning and parameter-efficient adaptation strategies provide limited practical benefit relative to their additional cost. These findings offer practical guidance for developing reproducible dense breast tissue segmentation models in mammography studies with limited labeled data.

title: A multi-scale cell-type resolved map of trans-regulatory architecture in the aging human brain
text: Mapping genetic effects on distal genes and regulatory programs is essential for understanding how genetic variation influences complex diseases; yet trans-QTL discovery remains limited by weak effect sizes, extensive multiple testing and poor reproducibility. Here, we introduce TransMap, a generalizable computational framework that combines multi-scale trans-QTL mapping with multi-phenotype genetic colocalization to improve the discovery and interpretation of distal regulatory variants. Beyond individual trans-eGenes, TransMap constructs local co-regulatory program phenotypes that account for background expression variation to improve the detection of weak, coordinated distal genetic effects. Across a broad range of simulation settings, TransMap achieved 9.2-36.7% higher trans-QTL discovery power than existing methods while maintaining well-controlled type I error rates. We applied TransMap to bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomic profiles from the aging human brain in the ADSP Functional Genomics Consortium (FunGen-AD), further integrating proteomic, glycoproteomic and metabolomic biomarker measurements (average N=476 donors). Genome-wide fine-mapping of TransMap single-gene and program-level QTL yielded variant annotations with 2.75-2.88x heritability enrichment across 57 complex diseases and traits (average N=307K), with complementary heritability information captured across regulatory scales. Multi-phenotype colocalization identified 49,532 trans-regulatory events supported by shared genetic signals with cis-eQTL or biomarker-QTL, including 1,825 candidate cis-trans-biomarker regulatory configurations. TransMap further revealed an asymmetric cross-cell-type regulatory architecture in which neuronal cis-regulatory signals preferentially associate with coordinated glial trans-regulatory responses, supported by co-culture experiments and spatial transcriptomics. Alzheimers disease (AD) GWAS-prioritized colocalization identified trans-regulatory associations in 115 AD-associated loci, including a KNOP1 cis-eQTL associated in trans with a microglial regulatory program containing MS4A4E, with additional support from statistical mediation analysis. TransMap provides a multi-scale, cell-type-resolved atlas of trans-regulatory variation and a generalizable framework for elucidating the regulatory architecture of complex diseases.

title: Investigating the potential effect of topiramate on anorexia nervosa and binge eating behaviour using drug-target Mendelian randomization
text: Topiramate is an antiseizure medication used to treat epilepsy and migraine and is commonly prescribed for appetite suppression and weight loss. However, whether its pharmacological actions influence eating disorder risk remains unclear. We applied drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) to investigate potential causal effects of topiramate on the risk of anorexia nervosa (AN; 24,223 cases and 1,243,971 controls) and binge-eating behaviour (BE; 39,279 cases and 1,227,436 controls) and, exploratorily, eight other psychiatric disorders: attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, anxiety disorders, alcohol use disorder, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and schizophrenia. We used summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR) to investigate genetically predicted pharmacological actions of topiramate using brain- and blood-derived cis-expression quantitative trait loci for genes encoding its molecular targets. Five genetic instruments consistent with topiramates antiepileptic action were validated: CA4 and CACNB3 expression in the brain and CA4, GRIK1, and GRIK3 expression in the blood. Robustness of the findings was assessed using SMR-multi, HEIDI, and colocalization analyses. After multiple-testing correction, genetically predicted inhibition of CA4 expression in blood was associated with decreased BE risk (OR = 0.867, 95% CI = 0.792-0.950, p = 0.002) and remained significant in SMR-multi (p = 0.0049). Colocalization provided moderate support for a shared causal variant underlying CA4 expression and BE (PPH4 = 0.58). No robust evidence was identified for AN or the eight exploratory psychiatric outcomes. Overall, our findings warrant further clinical and functional investigations into mechanisms underlying topiramate-associated appetite suppression and weight loss and their relevance to eating-disorder risk.

title: Molecular typing and characterisation of antimicrobial resistance determinants of Neisseria gonorrhoeae among symptomatic individuals in the Eastern Cape, South Africa
text: BackgroundAntimicrobial resistance in Neisseria gonorrhoeae threatens gonorrhoea treatment, while surveillance is constrained by limited culture capacity. We evaluated multi-antigen sequence typing (NG-MAST) and targeted real-time PCR for molecular epidemiology and detection of antimicrobial resistance-associated determinants directly from clinical specimens. MethodsWe analysed 235 N. gonorrhoeae-positive stored DNA extracts from symptomatic individuals in South Africa. NG-MAST sequence types were obtained directly or from whole-genome sequences (WGS) of paired cultured isolates. Real-time PCR targeted fluoroquinolone resistance-associated mutations (RAMs) in parC and gyrA and macrolide RAMs in the 23S rRNA gene. Results were compared with WGS and with phenotypic susceptibility results from paired isolates. ResultsNG-MAST sequence types were obtained for 200/235 (85.1%) specimens and were diverse, with ST21253 predominating (n=26). At least one gyrA or parC mutation was detected by real-time PCR in 110/193 (57.0%) specimens. Compared with WGS, positive agreement was 81.2% for parC and 97.0% for gyrA, and negative agreement 100% and 95.8%, respectively. Among 65 ciprofloxacin-resistant isolates, RAMs were detected in 60 (92.3%) by real-time PCR and 61 (93.8%) by WGS; four had no RAM detected by either method. The 23S rRNA C2611T mutation was detected by both methods in one isolate (azithromycin MIC, 8 mg/L); no A2059G mutations were detected. ConclusionsGonococcal sequence types were diverse, fluoroquinolone RAMs were common, and the assessed macrolide RAMs were rare. Real-time PCR applied directly to specimen DNA agreed well with WGS, but the targeted markers did not fully predict ciprofloxacin susceptibility, supporting complementary molecular and phenotypic approaches.

title: An early activated CD38highCD209highCD36low monocyte phenotype is associated with progression to severe dengue
text: BackgroundAlthough monocytes are among the principal target cells of dengue virus (DENV) infection we sought to investigate monocyte phenotypic markers associated with disease severity and evaluate their potential as prognostic biomarkers and therapeutic targets. MethodsDifferences in monocyte subpopulations and phenotypic markers were assessed by flow cytometry in patients with dengue fever (DF=33) and dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF=21) and compared to health controls (HCs=20). Further in vitro experiments were done by co-culturing peripheral blood mononucleocytes (PBMCs) of healthy individuals (n=8) with DENV2, DENV3, NS1 antigen of both serotypes and LPS. The changes in expression of CD36 and CD38 in vitro in monocytes were assessed. ResultsA significant expansion of intermediate monocytes and a contraction of the classical monocytes was seen in patients with DHF compared to DF and HCs, with no significant differences within the non-classical monocytes. Patients who progressed to develop DHF, exhibited an activated monocyte phenotype characterized by, expansion of CD38high, CD209high, CD86high, HLA-DRhigh, CD36low, intermediate monocyte subset. The highest expression of CD38 and CD86 was seen in non-classical monocytes, and CD209 and HLA-DR in intermediate monocytes. Most significant downregulation of CD36 was observed in non-classical monocytes. CD38 expression on monocytes (especially classical monocytes) positively and significantly correlated with liver transaminases and serum ferritin levels. Co-culture of PBMCs with DENV3 led to significant downregulation of CD36 (p=0.023). ConclusionsThese results suggest that early alterations in monocyte activation, antigen presentation, viral entry, and lipid sensing pathways contribute to dengue immunopathogenesis.

title: Single-cell profiling of human plaques reveals cellular and molecular signatures of symptomatic atherosclerosis
text: Atherosclerotic plaque vulnerability drives ischemic cardiovascular events, yet the cellular and molecular signatures distinguishing symptomatic from asymptomatic human plaques remain poorly defined. Here, we compared 53 symptomatic and asymptomatic human carotid plaques using single-nucleus (snRNA-seq; 17 samples, 19,100 nuclei; AtherOMICS biobank) and single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq; 36 samples, 68,983 cells; four public datasets), analyzed independently and combined by meta-analysis. Across sequencing approaches, symptomatic plaques showed cell-state shifts toward later or terminal states in osteochondrogenic smooth muscle cells (SMCs) and CD4 T cells, as well as transcriptional changes toward inflammatory and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in endothelial cells (ECs), T cells, and fibroblasts. Nuclear profiling uncovered a depletion of fibroblasts in symptomatic plaques, marked by downregulation of RGS5. Integrating these transcriptomic signatures with genome-wide association data for coronary, cerebrovascular, and peripheral atherosclerotic disease, we found that genetic risk was enriched primarily in vascular wall cells (SMCs, fibroblasts, ECs), rather than immune cell types. The analyses further nominated higher TWIST1 expression in ECs (colocalized with risk across four atherosclerotic phenotypes), lower GUCY1A1 expression in fibroblasts and macrophages, and higher MRAS expression in T cells as candidate driver mechanisms linking genetic risk to symptomatic plaque transition. These findings provide novel insights into cellular and molecular phenotypes associated with plaque vulnerability and identify potential driver mechanisms of symptomatic plaque transformation that could inform therapeutic development.

title: Insulin resistance reverses despite weight gain with pan-PPAR agonism, revealing its plasma molecular correlates in type 2 diabetes
text: Insulin resistance (IR) and body weight are closely linked in type 2 diabetes (T2D), so their molecular correlates are hard to separate in observational data. Pan-PPAR agonism offers a test, because it improves insulin sensitivity while body weight increases. In the ChiHOPE cohort of 835 T2D patients from two randomized phase 3 trials of chiglitazar, 53% of chiglitazar-treated patients with HOMA-IR-defined IR at baseline no longer met the IR threshold after treatment, compared with 29% with placebo and 32% with sitagliptin, while BMI rose. We integrated plasma metabolomics and proteomics into a molecular estimate of HOMA-IR. It outperformed routine clinical measures, disagreed with HOMA-IR classification in 27% of patients, and identified adverse lipid, liver and inflammatory profiles within each HOMA-IR class. With chiglitazar, the molecular estimate fell despite weight gain, with lower proteoglycan 4 and higher glutamine and glycine. Circulating markers of IR can therefore improve without weight loss. HighlightsO_LIChiglitazar reversed HOMA-IR-defined insulin resistance in about half of patients as BMI rises C_LIO_LIA plasma multi-omics score estimated HOMA-IR better than routine clinical measures C_LIO_LIThe molecular estimate enabled better stratification by HOMA-IR C_LIO_LIIR-linked plasma molecules improved despite weight gain, led by falling PRG4 C_LI

title: Accounting for Insulin-on-board in Large Language Model Advice about Pediatric Hyperglycemia
text: Large language models (LLMs) can be used by patients and caregivers to answer medical questions and the characterization of safety concerns in LLM outputs for patient-facing applications is an active area of research. In this work, we study LLM responses to caregiver questions about hyperglycemia in pediatric type 1 diabetes. We measure the frequency of a potential safety failure: advice to dose insulin in the absence of a clear warning to account for insulin-on-board. We found occurrences of the potential safety failure across four LLMs tested through programmatic endpoints and two LLMs tested through chat interfaces. The rates of the potential safety failure varied when different context was given about the patient's meal and insulin history and treatment regimen. These results highlight a need for guardrails for patients with diabetes who use LLMs to manage their care.

title: Persisting inequalities in past-year drug use by sexual identity: trends across England's 2007, 2014 and 2024 Adult Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys
text: IntroductionSexual minority people experience disproportionate discrimination and minority stress, contributing to poorer health and health-related behaviours, including drug use. Increasing drug potency and adulteration may heighten associated harms. UK evidence on sexual identity inequalities in drug use is dated, and whether inequalities have changed over time is unclear. MethodsAdult Psychiatric Morbidity Surveys 2007 (N=7403), 2014 (N=7546) and 2024 (N=6912) provide repeated cross-sectional probability samples of the household population of England. Weighted prevalence of past-year drug use was analysed by sexual identity, sex and age. Logistic regression adjusted for age, sex and area deprivation. Trends focused on 16-64-year-olds. ResultsIn 2024, past-year drug use among adults 16+ was reported by: 9.1% heterosexual, 18.3% gay/lesbian, 26.8% bisexual, 28.3% other identity adults. Among 16-64-year-olds, drug use in sexual minority adults (2007=22.9%, 2014=27.5%, 2024=24.9%) remained at least double that of heterosexual adults (2007=10.3%, 2014=9.9%, 2024=11.6%), with adjusted odds ratios of 2.4 (95% CI:1.7-3.2, 2007), 3.2 (2.2-4.8, 2014) and 2.2 (1.4-3.4, 2024). The gap between sexual minority and heterosexual women appeared to widen, although confidence intervals were wide. ConclusionsSexual identity inequalities in drug use persisted over 17 years in England. Prevention, treatment and policies should address these inequalities and their social determinants including discrimination and exclusion. Routine drug statistics should be reported by sexual identity. Health surveys should collect gender identity and be large enough to enable disaggregation of sexual and gender identities. HighlightsO_LIPast-year drug-use was more common in sexual minority than heterosexual adults C_LIO_LIOverall, odds remained at least double in sexual minority adults over the 17 years C_LIO_LISexual identity inequities evident for a range of drug types C_LIO_LIAmong women, sexual identity inequities in drug use may have widened C_LIO_LIHealth survey samples should be sufficient to explore age and sex intersections C_LI

title: Inferring viral variants and fitness advantages from longitudinal wastewater sequencing data
text: During the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic, wastewater-based epidemiology emerged as an effective tool for monitoring infection dynamics. However, wastewater represents a pooled sample of incomplete viral genomic fragments originating from multiple individuals in the catchment area of a wastewater treatment plant, preventing the assembly of complete viral genomes. Existing computational pipelines are therefore limited in detecting new variants that are absent from clinical sequencing data. We developed FitNMF, an integrated viral dynamics and non-negative matrix factorization model that leverages the temporal structure of wastewater sequencing data and the underlying variant competition to jointly infer mutational signatures, relative abundances, and fitness advantages of circulating variants directly from wastewater next-generation sequencing data. Using simulated data as well as wastewater time-series data collected between 2021 and 2024 across six Swiss wastewater treatment plants, we demonstrate FitNMFs ability to identify and quantify emerging variants de novo, offering a powerful tool for real-time variant surveillance in settings with limited clinical sequencing.

title: Repeated sleep-medication reporting patterns and cognitive change in HRS and SHARE
text: BackgroundSelf-reported sleep-medication use has been inconsistently linked to cognitive decline, largely because sleep disturbances, affective symptoms, and treatment transitions co-evolve over time. Moreover, whether repeated sleep-medication reports across consecutive survey waves follow a monotonic dose-response gradient with subsequent cognitive aging remains unclear. We evaluated baseline, two-wave, and three-wave longitudinal patterns of sleep-medication reporting in relation to cognitive trajectories across two large aging cohorts in the United States and Europe. MethodsWe analyzed population-based data from adults aged [≥]50 years in the US Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). First, we examined associations between baseline sleep-medication use and longitudinal changes in standardized global cognition and memory scores (Analysis 1: HRS n = 16,323; SHARE n = 41,453). Second, we conducted a prespecified two-wave landmark analysis classifying participants by reported sleep-medication use across two consecutive visits (HRS waves 11-12; SHARE waves 4-5) as 0, 1, or 2 use-positive visits, and by reporting sequence (00, 01, 10, and 11), with cognitive trajectories modeled from the second visit onward (Analysis 2: HRS n = 13,915; SHARE n = 29,214). Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and slopes adjusted for baseline sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical covariates and all covariate-by-time interactions. Third, we extended the landmark window to three consecutive visits (HRS waves 11-13, 2012-2016; SHARE waves 6-8, 2015-2020) to separate sustained from transient reporting, adjusting for interview mode and testing equivalence of sustained use to non-use (Analysis 3: HRS n = 12,310; SHARE n = 24,692). ResultsIn baseline analyses, sleep-medication use was associated with modestly faster decline in global cognition (HRS: {beta} = -0.0060 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0103 to -0.0017; SHARE: {beta} = -0.0034 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0070 to 0.0002) and memory (HRS: {beta} = -0.0062 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0115 to -0.0009; SHARE: {beta} = -0.0037 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0074 to 0.0001). In the two-wave landmark analysis, reporting sleep-medication use at both visits (2 vs 0 visits) was not associated with accelerated cognitive decline in either cohort, refuting a monotonic consistency gradient. Instead, reporting use at a single visit (1 vs 0 visits) was associated with steeper decline in Western Europe (global cognition: {beta} = -0.0087 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0157 to -0.0016; memory: {beta} = -0.0083 SD/year, 95% CI -0.0158 to -0.0007) and among SHARE participants with secondary/vocational or tertiary education (interaction P = 0.041 for global cognition and P = 0.017 for memory). In the three-wave extension, no exposure contrast survived familywise correction; sustained three-visit reporting was statistically equivalent to persistent non-use within {+/-}0.05 SD/year in both cohorts (equivalence P [≤] 0.0012). ConclusionsBaseline sleep-medication reporting was associated with small negative differences in cognitive trajectories, whereas a fixed two-wave landmark design did not support a monotonic cumulative-exposure gradient. The localization of steeper cognitive decline to intermittent (one-visit) reporting in Western Europe and higher educational strata points to the role of treatment transitions and symptom instability rather than sustained medication exposure. Three-wave, mode-adjusted and equivalence-tested analyses indicate that sustained sleep-medication reporting is not accompanied by accelerated cognitive decline at the population level, whereas transient reporting continues to mark periods of elevated risk.

title: Co-production of an oral health intervention: Enabling Service Users with Severe Mental Illness to Learn about and Engage (SMILE) with Good Oral Health
text: BackgroundPeople with severe mental illness (SMI) experience poorer oral health than the general population. They are less likely to visit the dentist or brush their teeth and face unique barriers to accessing oral health support. There is a limited number of oral health interventions for people with SMI, and there is no conclusive evidence on their effectiveness. An integrated oral health intervention delivered by mental health professionals in a community mental healthcare setting could offer a scalable option to oral health support for people with SMI. In this paper we report on the process of co-producing such an intervention in England. MethodsThe intervention development process was informed by Hawkins co-production framework. In this paper we report on stages 2 (co-production) and 3 (prototyping). Two online and two face-to-face co-production workshops took place (N=22) involving service users with SMI (n=6), mental health professionals (n=8) and dental health professionals (n=8). Two online patient and public involvement consultations, and a professional stakeholder meeting were held during the co-production process to provide feedback on the co-production process. The workshops informed the core components, format and content of the intervention. ResultsThe co-production process resulted in five intervention components: 1) Initiating a conversation about oral health, 2) providing advice to people with SMI on keeping their teeth and mouth healthy, 3) weekly tooth brushing text reminders, and 4) mental health professionals updating the care record to document the administration of this intervention. To support intervention delivery, we co-produced an intervention flowchart, an intervention leaflet for people with SMI, and a training manual for mental health professionals delivering the intervention. ConclusionWe co-produced an integrated oral health intervention to be delivered to service users with SMI in community mental health settings. The next stage of the research is a single-arm feasibility study to assess whether the intervention is acceptable to people with SMI and feasible to deliver within the NHS.

title: Rapid antidepressant effects of psilocybin without increased SV2A binding: baseline binding predicts response
text: We report a pre-registered [11C]UCB-J PET sub-study of a recently published randomized trial in which a single psilocybin dose produced rapid and sustained antidepressant effects in major depressive disorder (MDD). Synaptic loss has been implicated in MDD, and psychedelics induce synaptic remodeling in preclinical models within 24 hours, raising the possibility that psilocybins antidepressant effects involve increased synaptic density. We used the PET radioligand [11C]UCB-J targeting synaptic vesicle glycoprotein 2A (SV2A) to test this in thirty-five participants with moderate-to-severe recurrent MDD randomized 1:1 to a single dose of 25 mg psilocybin or 100 mg niacin placebo, both with psychotherapeutic support. [11C]UCB-J PET was performed 2-7 days before and 15 ({+/-}7) days after dosing. Despite significant clinical improvement in the psilocybin group, we found no evidence of a group-level increase in SV2A binding (VT or BPND) relative to niacin in the hippocampus or frontal cortex. In secondary analyses, higher baseline VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in the psilocybin group; this survived FDR correction at Day 8 and Day 15 (two of three pre-registered timepoints). Change in VT was associated with greater subsequent clinical improvement in unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated after adjustment for baseline VT and baseline MADRS and did not survive FDR correction. These findings indicate that substantial antidepressant improvement after psilocybin can occur without a detectable group-level increase in SV2A binding, while raising the possibility that baseline SV2A binding could help identify individuals more likely to respond.

title: Investigating Climate-Driven Disruption of Malaria Transmission Following the 2022 Sindh, Pakistan Floods: An Interrupted Time Series Study
text: Malaria remains a major global public health challenge in developing countries, with climate change intensifying its impact, particularly in vulnerable populations. Rising temperatures can expand the geographic range and local abundance of malaria vectors, Anopheles mosquitoes, which thrive in warm climates, with 25{degrees}C representing the optimal temperature for malaria transmission. In Pakistan, malaria is primarily spread through P. falciparum and P. vivax. Pakistan is one of the seven countries in the Eastern Mediterranean Region that accounts for 98% of the total malaria burden in the region. Recently, after catastrophic flooding in Pakistan in 2022 and the subsequent increase in malaria incidence, it has become imperative to estimate the climate change-attributed increase in the risk of malaria. In this study, we analyze the time series malaria case incidence data from the province of Sindh, Pakistan, and the climate data to quantify climate-attributed malaria cases in Sindh, Pakistan. We fit a negative binomial generalized linear model (GLM) to monthly case counts with interrupted time series and seasonality terms. The majority of malaria-confirmed infections were Plasmodium Vivax (40-95%) between 2016-2024, followed by Plasmodium falciparum infections. The positivity rate for malaria remained <10% until June 2022, and increased massively after the July 2022 flooding. After accounting for this case momentum, the onset of the 2022 floods was associated with an immediate, independent increase in malaria cases of approximately threefold (IRR 2.985, 95% CI 1.878-4.751, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that post-flooding malaria surveillance and response in flood-affected settings should anticipate not only an acute environmentally-driven surge in cases but also a subsequent period of elevated, self-sustaining transmission that may persist well beyond the resolution of the initiating environmental disruption, in this case the flooding.

title: Acceptability and feasibility of measles vaccination, small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplementation, and their co-delivery among children aged 6-23 months in northern Nigeria: a qualitative study
text: BackgroundUndernutrition and infectious diseases form a vicious cycle that endangers child survival in low-resource settings, including in Northern Nigeria. The NutriVax-Measles trial was designed to evaluate a strategy combining preventive small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) distributions with community mobilization and routine immunization services for children aged 6-23 months to improve measles vaccination uptake. To inform future programs co-delivering nutrition supplementation and immunization services at scale, we aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of measles vaccination, SQ-LNS distribution, and the NutriVax strategy. MethodsA qualitative study was conducted at the end of the trial using in-depth interviews (n=53) and focus group discussions (n=8) with key stakeholders: caregivers, health care workers, community health workers, and community representatives. Thematic analysis was guided by multiple conceptual frameworks. ResultsThe majority of the participants expressed satisfaction with measles vaccines in both arms, and with SQ-LNS in the NutriVax arm, as they perceived the benefits for their childrens health. In both arms, community awareness sessions and previous experience of outbreaks were key to motivating caregivers to bring their children to healthcare centres. Although distance to health facilities was identified as one of the main barriers to accessing care, SQ-LNS was perceived as an important source of motivation to bring their child to the clinic where they subsequently received vaccination. All stakeholder groups emphasized the importance of community leaders support and targeted male sensitization to address the prevailing sociocultural norms. Additionally, improved service organization to reduce waiting time was considered crucial to enhance caregivers acceptability of the intervention. ConclusionBoth measles vaccination and SQ-LNS provision were acceptable and feasible, supporting the NutriVax strategy within primary healthcare settings in fragile health systems. Successful implementation depends on sustained community sensitization, continued engagement of fathers and community leaders, and service delivery decentralized as close as possible to beneficiaries. KEY MESSAGESO_ST_ABSWhat is already known?C_ST_ABSO_LICo-delivering small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) with routine immunization is an effective strategy to improve vaccination coverage in Northern Nigeria. Yet, evidence on how vaccination and SQ-LNS are perceived, implemented, and experienced by stakeholders at health-care and community levels remains scarce. C_LIO_LIPersistent barriers to vaccination included socio-cultural misconceptions, gender norms, long waiting time and distance to health facilities. C_LI What do the new findings imply?O_LISustained community engagement, including targeted male sensitization, is important to improve measles vaccination acceptability. C_LIO_LISuccessful implementation of co-delivery programs also requires well-organized service delivery, with services decentralized to health facilities as close as possible to beneficiaries, particularly to reduce travel distances and waiting times.
