Four encoder-based transformer models were evaluated for aneurysm-presence classification using 5-fold stratified cross-validation. A zero-shot Llama 3.1 framework was used to extract aneurysm size using direct and structured-report prompting. RadDistilBERT and Llama 3.1 were evaluated on 20 temporally distinct reports using full-report and impression-only inputs, with and without structured preprocessing. Results RadDistilBERT achieved the highest mean classification performance, with accuracy of 96.4% (± 1.8%), F1 score of 91.7% (± 10.3%), precision of 94.0% (± 4.6%), and recall of 90.7% (± 15.6%). F1 scores were 87.5% for BERT-base-uncased and 31.1% for ALBERT-base-v2. In the 20-report set, aneurysm-presence classification accuracy was 100% across all input and processing conditions. For aneurysm size extraction, structured report processing increased accuracy from 61.90% to 66.67% using the full report and from 80.95% to 85.00% using the impression section. Conclusions This study demonstrates the feasibility of a dual-model transformer framework for aneurysm-presence classification and size extraction from unstructured neuroimaging reports. RadDistilBERT achieved the strongest classification performance, while Llama 3.1 enabled zero-shot size extraction. These findings support further external validation and expansion to additional aneurysm characteristics with dedicated annotation and validation.

title: Centralized vehicle-to-grid coordination for behind-the-meter value in commercial fleets: Evidence and deployment lessons from a pilot demonstration
text: Vehicle-to-grid operation in commercial fleets remains debated due to interoperability limits, user acceptance, warranty concerns, and regulatory uncertainty. This paper reports a five-week multi-site pilot demonstration in mainland Portugal evaluating a centralized coordination architecture that uses V2G and low-complexity rule-based control to capture behind-the-meter value: energy arbitrage under time-of-use tariffs, peak-load shaving, and photovoltaic surplus self-consumption, relying only on site telemetry, charging-session data, and conservative state-of-charge (SoC) limits agreed with fleet users. Across three sites, 374 kWh of charging was shifted from peak to off-peak periods, 150 kWh was discharged during peak periods, and 16.6 kWh of additional charging was enabled from solar surplus. These actions resulted in €20 of EV charging cost savings (a 26% cost-weighted reduction against the rebased baseline), €7.9 of site-level energy savings, and an estimated €39.4 reduction in demand-related charges, modest and highly site-specific values. Average departure SoC decreased from 96% to 79% but remained above the agreed 50% minimum throughout the pilot. Beyond these outcomes, the study draws deployment lessons on measurement uncertainty, control-interval limits, plug-in behavior, battery-condition observability, protocol maturity, deployment cost, and regulatory constraints.

title: From interoperable data to continuous care: a responsive implementation approach to personal health data spaces
text: Personal health data spaces (PHDSs) promise to give individuals meaningful control over longitudinal health information while making heterogeneous data available across settings of care.The promise is consequential: continuity may improve when a person can authorize access to clinical records, patient-reported information, wearable data, and other sources without each transition requiring a new reconstruction of the record. Yet technical availability is not equivalent to continuity. A PHDS can be interoperable, secure, and formally patient-controlled while remaining difficult to use, weakly integrated into clinical work, or unevenly accessible. The central challenge is therefore not only to build PHDSs, but to implement them so that data become usable relationships and coordinated action.The articles in this Research Topic make that challenge visible from complementary directions. Ambalavanan et al. propose a modular, ontology-driven front-end architecture linking user experience, security, data management, interoperability, analytics, and scalability (1). Lin et al. describe a blockchain-supported dynamic consent framework through which participants can modify permissions and data uses over time (2). Ruan et al., studying a population at high risk of stroke, show that proactive health behavior is associated with health literacy, social support, self-efficacy, and material circumstances (3). Read together, these contributions suggest that a technically capable data space will produce continuity only through an implementation system that makes participation understandable, supported, actionable, and revisable.This Opinion argues for a responsive implementation approach to PHDSs, in which technical capabilities, governance arrangements, organizational workflows, user supports, and learning processes are deliberately connected to improve care continuity. The SPHERE model -Social Prescribing and Health Equity through Responsive Evaluation -was developed for policies enabling social prescribing, not for digital health architecture (4). Its value here is therefore not as a template to transfer wholesale. Rather, its eight-part logic offers a useful viewpoint: durable effects emerge when foundations, infrastructure, community co-production, context, implementation strategies, process measures, outcomes, and feedback loops are deliberately connected. Applying that logic to PHDSs shifts the evaluative question from whether a data space exists to how, for whom, under what conditions, and through which mechanisms it improves continuity, and how implementation should be revised as evidence and surrounding conditions change.PHDS discussions often separate technical design from "adoption," treating implementation as a downstream step. This division is misleading. Decisions about identity verification, consent granularity, provenance displays, terminology services, access delegation, and clinical integration distribute work and authority among patients, caregivers, clinicians, organizations, and data stewards. They are implementation decisions because they shape who can participate, what actions are feasible, and whether the technology fits existing routines. Frameworks such as the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and NASSS similarly emphasize that technologies interact with recipients, organizations, wider systems, and change over time (5,6). Human-factors approaches further show that outcomes arise from interactions among people, tasks, tools, organizational conditions, and environments rather than from any component alone (7).Ambalavanan et al.'s layered architecture illustrates the point (1). Semantic standards may allow data to travel and be interpreted consistently, while a patient-centered front end can make provenance, consent status, and longitudinal information visible. Yet a provenance indicator may increase trust when its meaning is clear, add burden when it is not, or be ignored when clinicians lack tim

title: SmartKrishi-AI: A Survey of AI-Integrated Agriculture Decision Support and Farm Resource Management
text: Agricultural choices depend heavily on a complex mix of environmental variables, including soil properties, fluctuating weather patterns, crop compatibility, market dynamics, pest threats, and the availability of vital farming resources. Most contemporary digital services target only one of these factors, forcing growers to manually gather data from multiple disconnected websites and local contacts. This paper reviews recent developments related to SmartKrishi–AI, a conceptual, integrated platform designed for agricultural decision-making and asset coordination. Our analysis evaluates several vital domains, including crop recommendation frameworks, weather forecasting networks, commodity price models, plant disease diagnostics, public welfare discovery, equipment leasing, and labor scheduling. We analyze recent research from 2023 to 2026 indexed across major venues such as IEEE, Elsevier/ScienceDirect, and MDPI, exploring their mathematical approaches, dataset constraints, evaluation methods, and practical challenges. Based on these insights, we introduce a conceptual multilayer architecture that connects data-driven analytical models with verified institutional channels and peer-to-peer resource exchange workflows. Because the proposed ecosystem serves as a structural blueprint rather than an experimentally fieldtested software tool, no project-specific crop yield or predictive precision increases are claimed. Finally, we highlight persistent open challenges in this sector, such as data quality gaps, geographic adaptation limits, model interpretability, forecast volatility, system interoperability, regional language support, and the necessity for rigorous field trials.

title: Translation of policy into practice: a qualitative exploratory study of digitally supported antimicrobial stewardship programs in Nepalese hospitals
text: Abstract Background Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents an escalating public health crisis worldwide, with low- and middle-income countries bearing a disproportionate burden. Nepal has developed its National Action Plan on AMR (2024–2028), yet translating policy into functional hospital-based antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs), particularly those supported by digital health tools, remains a formidable challenge. This study explored the facilitators and barriers to implementing digitally supported ASPs in Nepalese hospitals from the perspectives of diverse health system stakeholders. Methods A qualitative exploratory study was conducted using an interpretivist approach. Semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted with 38 purposively selected participants. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. Reporting adhered to the Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research (COREQ) checklist. Results Four overarching themes emerged: (1) perceptions and awareness of AMR, characterized by recognition of AMR as an urgent crisis driven by inappropriate prescribing, unregulated community antibiotic access, and One Health determinants; (2) current antimicrobial use practices and systemic challenges, including the dominance of empirical prescribing, variable guideline adherence, and ASP structures constrained by inadequate manpower and authority; (3) feasibility and acceptability of digital health tools for ASP, revealing broad support for digital integration alongside concerns about system fragmentation, variable institutional digital maturity, and the insistence that digital tools should support rather than replace clinical judgment; and (4) barriers, facilitators, and recommendations for sustainable ASP implementation, highlighting workforce shortages, leadership commitment, policy alignment, interoperability standards, and the need for sustained investment in both human resources and digital infrastructure. Conclusion While awareness of AMR and initial ASP structures exists across Nepalese hospitals, effective and sustainable implementation requires coordinated action spanning clinical, laboratory, digital, and policy domains. Digital health tools offer considerable promise for strengthening stewardship activities, but their successful integration depends on resolving foundational issues of interoperability, workforce capacity, standardization, and sustained leadership commitment. These findings provide concrete, pillar-specific entry points for operationalizing Nepal’s revised National Action Plan on AMR (2024–2028).

title: On-device reinforcement learning-based insulin dosing controller for fully automated insulin delivery
text: Introduction Automated insulin delivery (AID) systems integrate continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) with algorithm-driven insulin dosing to enable closed-loop glycemic management for people with type 1 diabetes (T1D). Recent advances in wearable glucose sensing and insulin delivery technologies have enabled increasingly compact AID systems; however, deploying advanced AI-based dosing algorithms directly on resource-constrained wearable devices remains technically challenging. Some AID architectures also rely on external devices, such as smartphones or dedicated controllers, introducing additional communication dependencies into the closed-loop operation. Methods This study presents an on-device insulin dosing controller based on the soft actor–critic (SAC) algorithm for resource-constrained AID systems. The proposed approach processes CGM data and makes insulin dosing decisions locally, without relying on external computing devices. To enable embedded deployment, a compressed SAC architecture with a lightweight encoder was developed using quantization-aware training and knowledge distillation, together with an online adaptation mechanism for individualized control. The controller was implemented on a resource-constrained microcontroller and evaluated in a hardware-in-the-loop framework using virtual patients from a T1D simulator. Results The proposed controller achieved an average time-in-range of 83% while maintaining real-time on-device execution with millijoule-level energy consumption per control step. Discussion These hardware-in-the-loop and in-silico results demonstrate the technical feasibility of real-time reinforcement learning-based insulin dosing and personalization on a resource-constrained embedded platform, while clinical efficacy and safety require further validation.

title: A Survey on LLMs from a Human-Centric Perspective
text: The rapid evolution of large language models (LLMs) has positioned them as powerful computational instruments for human-centered research and applications, spanning tasks involving cognition, decision-making, and social interaction. This survey examines LLMs from a human-centric perspective organized around individual and collective levels. We first review LLM competencies across perception, analysis, integration, execution, and social interaction, highlighting both their demonstrated capabilities and the evaluation conditions under which these capabilities are observed. We then explore how LLMs are used across behavioral science, psychology, linguistics, political science, economics, and sociology as research tools, behavioral simulators, and objects of inquiry, covering both individual behavior and collective social processes. Finally, we identify challenges and future research directions, such as improving LLM adaptability, affective-to-behavior evaluation, and cultural sensitivity, while addressing inherent biases and enhancing frameworks for human-AI collaboration. This survey aims to provide a foundational understanding of LLMs from a human-centric perspective, offering insights into their current capabilities and potential for future development.

title: Rule Forest: Interpretable Ensembles of LLM-Generated Questions for Rare-Outcome Prediction
text: Many high-stakes screening decisions in finance amount to predicting a rare outcome from unstructured text, such as whether a founder will successfully build a large company, or which crowdfunded loan will fail to attract funding. When positives are this rare, simple models may be preferable to more complex ones. For example, a model that learns a weight for each feature may have too little signal to estimate those weights reliably, and also inspecting the model means reading a list of fitted coefficients rather than a simple rule that can be checked by eye. We introduce Rule Forest, which uses a large language model to generate simple YES/NO questions, rather than using it to directly predict outcomes, and combines the strongest questions into an equal-weight "green-flags" scorecard. This scorecard is as accurate as an equivalent model that learns a weight per question, within noise, and its advantage appears largest when positives are rarest. The result is an interpretable list of rules that a domain expert can edit and extend. When predicting founder success, the fraction of shortlisted founders who succeed increases from about 1 in 50 to 1 in 10, and to about 1 in 6 with a handful of expert-written questions. A second dataset which focuses on identifying failed loans, Kiva microloans, shows the same qualitative pattern. Across both tasks, the lesson is the same: a language model is most useful not as the predictor but as a generator of features a person can read, edit, and improve, and when positives are scarce that interpretability costs no measurable accuracy.

title: Generalizable Operating Room Expert with Multimodal Enhancement
text: Precise spatial modeling in the operating room (OR) is essential for intraoperative awareness, hazard avoidance, and surgical decision-making. Although existing approaches exploit multimodal data to learn spatial relationships, many depend on sensing modalities that are difficult to deploy in real clinical environments and remain limited in explicit 3D reasoning under constrained sensing conditions. Meanwhile, models trained primarily on readily available 2D data often fail to capture the fine-grained geometric and semantic structure of complex OR scenes. To address these limitations, we introduce OR-Expert, a large vision-language framework for 3D spatial reasoning with RGB-only inference. OR-Expert internally derives depth, panoptic segmentation, and point-cloud cues from RGB images and encodes them as structured spatial representations. Its Spatial-Enhanced Feature Fusion Block aligns these pseudo-modalities with RGB and textual features in a shared token space, enabling joint semantic, geometric, and language reasoning. The unified end-to-end MLLM therefore supports detailed spatial understanding without requiring external depth, segmentation, or point-cloud sensors, or additional expert annotations at inference time. Experiments on multiple operating-room benchmarks demonstrate that OR-Expert achieves state-of-the-art performance and generalizes effectively to unseen surgical scenes and downstream spatial reasoning tasks.

title: Immune interaction signatures in adipose tissue fibroblasts in obesity-associated atherosclerosis.
text: Atherosclerosis involves changes in the vascular wall and surrounding perivascular adipose tissue, yet the cellular contributors to disease progression remain incompletely understood. Obesity exacerbates atherogenesis, but the cell types driving this aggravation are unclear. We aimed to define the key cell populations across tissues in a highly atherogenic mouse model under obese and normal-weight conditions and to identify obesity-associated cellular changes. We employed 5' single-cell RNA sequencing combined with antibody staining in Ldlr-/- Apob100/100 male mice fed either a high-fat or control diet. Aorta, perivascular and epididymal adipose tissues, and spleen were analyzed, with CD45+ enrichment of aortic samples and CITE-seq using a 138-antibody panel. Key findings were validated in mice by immunohistochemistry and multiplexed immunofluorescence and explored in human aorta and carotid arteries using spatial transcriptomics. Analysis of ∼46,000 cells enabled characterization of cell states, gene enrichment, regulon activity, and inferred interactions. Adipose-derived fibroblast subsets displayed immune-associated transcriptional programs in obesity. The frequency of PI16+ progenitor fibroblasts was reduced per unit area, alongside marked PVAT remodelling, and the top mouse differentially expressed genes exhibited clear spatial patterning in human arteries.

title: Graph learning guided by regulatory and spatial contexts prioritizes natural compound-target pairs in digestive system cancers.
text: Heterogeneity in tumor regulatory programs, cellular composition and spatial organization complicates target prioritization for natural compounds. We developed a spatial-context heterogeneous graph neural network ranker (SC-HGNN-Rank) that combines relation-aware graph representations with ranking optimization to integrate compound-target associations, transcriptional regulation, interaction networks, and single-cell and spatial information. The model ranked 600 candidate axes in colon adenocarcinoma (COAD), hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC) and gastric adenocarcinoma (STAD). Under matched training conditions, mean Spearman correlations with the reference ranking were 0.965, 0.967 and 0.976 for leave-one-cancer-out, compound-group holdout and target-group holdout evaluations, respectively. The composite ranking objective improved mean Spearman correlation by 0.049 over a simple objective using the same encoder, whereas removing the spatial module reduced it by 0.147. Model ranking and multilayer evidence prioritized Quercetin-CDK1/MYB-Myeloid in COAD, 4',5-dihydroxyflavone (4',5-DHF)-AR/HDAC1-T/NK in LIHC, and Eriodyctiol-HSP90AB1/HOPX-Fibroblast in STAD. Expanded spatial analyses with expression-matched gene controls assessed associations between target expression and mapped cell abundance. Cellular thermal shift and drug affinity responsive target stability assays showed increased retention of target proteins after compound treatment. In HCT116, JHH-6 and MKN45 cells, the compounds reduced viability, colony formation, migration and invasion cell counts, and increased apoptosis. Target knockdown produced similar growth-inhibitory phenotypes, whereas overexpression attenuated compound-induced effects, supporting the involvement of CDK1, AR and HSP90AB1 in the respective responses. The accompanying Explorer supports candidate searches, evidence inspection and data export. By incorporating regulatory and spatial contexts into natural-compound prioritization, this study provides a reusable approach and experimentally supported candidates for target-directed pharmacological research in digestive system cancers.

title: Targeting Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases in Cancer: Dual Roles and Therapeutic Implications.
text: Protein Tyrosine Phosphatases (PTPs) play a dual role in cancer as both tumor suppressors and oncogenic drivers by dephosphorylating key signaling molecules. They take part in core oncogenic pathways, either suppressing tumor formation or promoting cancer progression through proliferation and immune suppression. Recent therapeutic advances have explored allosteric inhibitors, degraders and combination approaches targeting non-catalytic regulatory domains or the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Combined with immune checkpoint blockade, these strategies have potential to resolve selectivity limitations of traditional catalytic-site inhibitors alongside hard-to-target and dual-role challenges. This paper proposes a paradigm shift from single enzyme activity inhibition to microenvironment regulation and combination strategies, emphasizing the need to target non-catalytic regions and integrate the Tumor Microenvironment (TME) using single-cell spatial transcriptomics and biomarker analysis to advance combinations of PTP inhibitors and immune checkpoint inhibitors from preclinical models toward early-phase clinical investigation. METHOD: We conducted a narrative review of PubMed through October 2026 and hand-searched reference lists of relevant guidelines, reviews, and primary studies. We prioritized international guidance, systematic reviews, multicenter registries, prospective cohorts, and clinically informative mechanistic studies. Case reports and experimental studies were kept when they addressed questions not covered by higher-level evidence. The review was not protocol driven and did not include duplicate screening, formal risk-of-bias assessment, or a PRISMA flow diagram.

title: Advances in natural product inhibitors targeting the type III secretion system 1 of Salmonella.
text: Salmonella is an important foodborne pathogen that poses significant threats to human health, animal production, and food safety. Increasing antimicrobial resistance and limitations of conventional control strategies have promoted the development of anti-virulence approaches targeting bacterial virulence factors. The type III secretion system 1 (T3SS-1) mediates Salmonella invasion into host cells and effector protein translocation, yet is dispensable for bacterial survival, rendering it a promising anti-virulence target. This review summarizes recent advances in natural product-derived T3SS-1 inhibitors, classifies relevant inhibitors based on chemical structural characteristics and, from a mechanistic perspective, distinguishes direct protein binding mode with well-defined molecular interactions from indirect regulation mode that exert modulatory effects. It further explores the structure-activity relationships (SAR) between the structural features of natural products and their anti-virulence activities, aiming to provide theoretical bases for the discovery and optimization of novel anti-virulence lead compounds.

title: Advancing population-based cancer registries through the OHDSI OMOP Common Data Model: governance, validation, and interoperability for cancer research.
text: Population-based cancer registries (PBCRs) are essential for cancer surveillance and research but are limited in their analytical interoperability with other data sources because of heterogeneity in cancer-related definitions and database structure. The Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) can be used to improve interoperability between PBCRs and other health data. In this perspective, we provide a conceptual framework of how governance contributes to consistent mapping, validation, and sustainable use of OMOP CDM for PBCRs. We also demonstrate a newly developed R/Shiny validation tool that supports transparency and trust in the converted registry data. When OMOP CDMs are implemented with structured governance, it can support scalable, reproducible, multisite research and contribute to the readiness for the upcoming European Health Data Space regulation. Likewise, PBCRs advance cancer research and surveillance and contribute to the creation of a trusted, interoperable health data ecosystem that supports research and policy-making.

title: Implementation of the Toronto guidelines for childhood cancer staging: experience from 65 population-based cancer registries participating in the BENCHISTA project.
text: Population-based cancer registries (PBCRs) are central to measuring childhood cancer outcomes and informing global health policy. The International Benchmarking of Childhood Cancer Survival by Stage (BENCHISTA) project stimulated participating PBCRs to assign stage at diagnosis according to the international Toronto Stage Guidelines (TGs). This study aims to provide a quantitative assessment of operational findings and structural barriers limiting routine TGs implementation within PBCRs participating in the first phase of BENCHISTA. Seventy-three PBCRs participating in the first phase of BENCHISTA were invited to complete a semistructured survey assessing operational practices, data collection capacity, and structural and operational barriers to routine implementation of the TGs and associated non-stage-prognostic (NSP) variables across six solid childhood tumours. Sixty-five PBCRs from 23 countries provided valid and complete answers. Before BENCHISTA, 85% PBCRs reported no routine collection of TGs. Following participation, 51% indicated that they would continue staging all childhood cancers. The principal barriers to TGs assignment were workload (38%), lack of linkage with clinical sources (32%), and time required for data retrieval (29%). Molecular NSP variables-particularly rhabdomyosarcoma fusion markers and medulloblastoma subgroups-were the most difficult to capture due to inconsistent pathology reporting and limited registry access to molecular data. Fewer than half had systematic collection of treatment and recurrence data. This multinational survey provides a quantitative assessment of barriers limiting routine TGs implementation in PBCRs. Sustaining consistent data collection will require targeted investment in workforce capacity, improved interoperability between clinical and registry systems, and standardisation of clinical, molecular, and pathology reporting frameworks.

title: AI in Neuro-Oncology: A Review in Neuroimaging.
text: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become central to neuro-oncological imaging, impacting clinical and scientific workflows. In clinical practice, AI-based image reconstruction and noise reduction expedite the generation of advanced multiparametric MRI and PET scans. Automated segmentation and volumetric analysis improve reproducibility, speed, and standardization of tumor quantification and response assessment. In research, large language and multimodal models extract structured information from radiology reports and medical records. Collaborative initiatives, such as BraTS and FeTS, have established standardized, privacy-compliant frameworks for large-scale quantitative analyses. Tumor-specific applications include noninvasive molecular profiling in gliomas, grading and recurrence prediction in meningiomas, detection and response assessment in brain metastases, and pediatric-specific modeling aligned with RAPNO. However, AI models remain sensitive to technical and biological variations across institutions, limiting their clinical utility unless appropriate training and validation is performed. Nevertheless, progress is evident in prospective, biopsy-validated infiltration mapping, assessment of resection extent aligned with RANO-Resect, and standardization through AI-RANO. Emerging directions include foundation models, uncertainty estimation, federated learning, AI-enhanced ultra-low-field MRI, and dual-tracer PET. When used as a decision-support tool rather than a replacement for the imaging team, AI can increasingly improve the utility, reproducibility, and efficiency of quantitative, multiparametric imaging in patients with brain tumors. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to analyze brain scans of patients with brain tumors. AI can improve image quality, speed up acquisition, and automatically measure tumors, thereby making image analysis faster and more consistent. In research, AI can extract information from medical reports. International collaborations enable large-scale studies while protecting privacy. AI may help predict tumor features, aggressiveness, recurrence, and treatment response in both adults and children. However, tools trained at one hospital may perform poorly elsewhere, so careful testing is essential. AI works best as an assistant to doctors, not a replacement.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Behavioral Phenotyping: From Behavioral Neuroscience to Depression Research.
text: Behavioral phenotyping remains the main experimental readout for investigating brain function and neuropsychiatric disease. However, conventional behavioral analysis relies largely on manually defined endpoints that simplify the multidimensional nature of behavior and often overlook subtle behavioral dynamics. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL) and computer vision, are fundamentally transforming this landscape by enabling automated, high-resolution quantification of behavior across species and experimental paradigms. This review discusses recent developments in AI-based behavioral phenotyping and their implications for translational neuroscience, with particular emphasis on emerging applications to depression research. We first describe how markerless pose estimation has changed movement quantification, followed by supervised and unsupervised ML approaches that classify predefined behaviors or discover latent behavioral motifs directly from movement data. We then discuss how these approaches are reshaping systems neuroscience by enabling increasingly detailed descriptions of behavioral organization and facilitating the investigation of behavior as a continuous, multidimensional process. Finally, we examine their application to experimental models and clinical studies of depression, considering their potential and the limitations of translating computational behavioral measures across experimental and clinical settings. AI-based behavioral phenotyping represents an important methodological advance in neuroscience, shifting behavioral analysis from the quantification of isolated experimental endpoints toward the characterization of integrated behavioral states. In depression research, these approaches may improve behavioral characterization in experimental models and provide quantitative measures of clinically-relevant behavioral alterations in humans. However, linking experimental and clinical phenotypes will require methodological standardization, independent validation, and careful evaluation of cross-species comparability.

title: Rapid assessment of authenticity and quality of Ziziphi Spinosae semen using multi-source information fusion technology and intelligent sensory technologies.
text: Ziziphi Spinosae Semen (ZSS), a medicinal and edible herb, is often adulterated for economic gain, posing risks to product quality and consumer health. To address this challenge, we developed a multi-source intelligent sensory system integrating electronic eye, electronic nose, and FT-NIR spectroscopy, combined with information fusion strategies for both qualitative and quantitative analysis of ZSS adulteration. For authentication, partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), least squares support vector machine (LS-SVM), and convolutional neural network (CNN) models were built; for quantification, partial least squares regression (PLSR) was used to predict adulteration ratios and marker compound contents. Both single-source and fused models achieved 100% accuracy in distinguishing authentic, adulterated, and counterfeit samples. Quantitative results showed that the fused model predicted the adulteration ratio of Hovenia acerba seeds (HAS) with a MAPE of 0.86% (R2 = 0.9965), while a single-source model performed best for Ziziphus mauritiana seeds (ZMS). For jujuboside A and B, the fused model yielded a MAPE of 4.42% (R2 = 0.8799) and a MAPE of 4.01% (R2 = 0.9002), respectively. This rapid method offers a reliable tool for ZSS quality control in food and herbal medicine industries.

title: Development and external validation of an explainable machine-learning model for the prediction of unfavourable clinical-radiological outcome at three months in thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fractures.
text: No externally validated tools stratify three-month prognosis after thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fracture. An explainable logistic-regression model with nine predictors achieved an external AUC-ROC of 0.744 (sensitivity 90.7%). The counterfactual analysis of vertebral augmentation, the only modifiable predictor, is hypothesis-generating and should not be interpreted as a treatment recommendation. Thoracolumbar osteoporotic vertebral fractures (OVF) carry substantial morbidity and mortality, yet no externally validated tool stratifies three-month prognosis. We developed and externally validated an explainable machine-learning model for the three-month unfavourable clinical-radiological outcome. Retrospective observational study reported according to TRIPOD. Unfavourable outcome was defined as persistent pain, progression of vertebral height loss and/or worsening of independence in daily activities. A derivation cohort of 482 patients aged ≥50 years with acute thoracolumbar OVF treated at a tertiary centre (2017-2021) was used to train and internally validate seven algorithms with hyperparameter optimisation and stratified fivefold cross-validation. An independent two-centre cohort (n = 74) was used for external validation without retraining. Interpretability was based on SHAP values. The unfavourable outcome occurred in 53.9% of the derivation cohort and 58.1% of the external cohort. A nine-variable logistic-regression model with Platt calibration was selected (cross-validated AUC-ROC 0.675, 95% CI 0.622-0.728; external AUC-ROC 0.744, 95% CI 0.628-0.844). At the pre-specified internal Youden threshold (0.556), external sensitivity was 60.5% and specificity 71.0%; at a post-hoc external threshold (0.432), 90.7% and 54.8% (Brier 0.211, expected calibration error 0.096). Vertebral augmentation was the strongest and only modifiable predictor (mean |SHAP | = 0.278); counterfactual analysis showed an absolute risk reduction of 17.1-26.6 percentage points (median 25.3). The model predicts the three-month outcome of thoracolumbar OVF with an external AUC-ROC of 0.744 and preserved calibration. The counterfactual analysis of vertebral augmentation is hypothesis-generating and not a treatment recommendation; larger external validation, long-term outcomes and harm assessment are required before clinical use.

title: Utilizing machine learning to predict functional recovery, complications, adjacent segment disease and fusion status after cervical spine surgery: a systematic review.
text: Postoperative outcomes following cervical spine surgery remain heterogeneous, limiting effective preoperative risk stratification. Conventional prognostic approaches rely on demographic, clinical, and qualitative imaging factors but incompletely capture complex, high-dimensional information present in modern imaging. Machine learning-based imaging models have emerged as promising tools for individualized outcome prediction; however, the scope, performance, and methodological quality of this literature have not been systematically synthesized. A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed and Scopus were searched from inception through November 2025 for English-language studies applying machine learning or artificial intelligence techniques to imaging data to predict postoperative outcomes following cervical spine surgery. Data on study design, imaging modality, model architecture, validation strategy, performance metrics, and risk of bias (PROBAST) were extracted and synthesized narratively. The search identified 117 records, of which 16 studies published between 2021 and 2025 met inclusion criteria after full-text or detailed eligibility review. Studies addressed prediction of functional or neurologic recovery (7 studies), postoperative complications (4 studies), adjacent segment degeneration or disease (2 studies), utilization or biomechanical recovery metrics (2 studies), and fusion status assessment (1 study). Sample sizes ranged from 47 to 945 patients. Most studies used internal validation only, reported discrimination metrics, and demonstrated high or unclear risk of bias on PROBAST, primarily within the analysis domain. Machine learning-based imaging models show promise for improving prediction of postoperative outcomes following cervical spine surgery, particularly for neurologic recovery and complication risk. However, most existing models rely on internal validation and demonstrate methodological limitations that restrict clinical translation. Rigorous external validation, standardized imaging workflows, and improved reporting of calibration and clinical utility are needed before these approaches can be responsibly integrated into routine practice.

title: Advanced drug delivery strategies for overcoming tumor-mediated molecular hijacking: Emerging nanotherapeutics, advanced biotherapeutics, and artificial intelligence.
text: Recent advances in precision oncology fueled the development of nanotherapeutics,​ molecularly targeted drugs, engineered immunotherapies, RNA therapeutics, and smart biomaterials for more selective cancer treatment. However, long-term therapeutic responses remain restricted by interconnected adaptive mechanisms, including ABC transporter-mediated drug efflux, dysregulated signaling pathways, apoptosis evasion, immune escape, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and tumor microenvironment​ remodeling. In this review article, these processes are collectively framed as tumor-mediated molecular hijacking, describing malignant cell exploitation and microenvironmental pathways that promote multidrug resistance and therapeutic failure. The review critically examines nanotherapeutic and advanced biotherapeutic strategies to counteract these mechanisms, including functionalized nanocarriers, antibody-drug conjugates, CAR-T cells, tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, immune checkpoint blockade, mesenchymal stem-cell (MSC)-based therapeutics, CRISPR-mediated genome editing, bispecific T-cell engagers, and RNA-based approaches. Particular focus includes drug-delivery elements such as tumour penetration, intracellular trafficking, controlled release, pharmacokinetics, biodistribution, and critical formulation attributes, as well as translational challenges such as manufacturability, scalability, reproducibility, stability, safety, and regulatory feasibility. Emerging biofabrication approaches enable the fabrication of adaptive and personalized delivery systems, while artificial intelligence and machine learning are utilized as tools for structure-guided design, nanocarrier optimization, treatment-response prediction, and patient-specific digital-twin modelling. This paper combines tumor-mediated molecular hijacking with drug delivery technology at the forefront and translational aspects to create a comprehensive platform for clinically relevant precision cancer therapeutics.Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

title: Navigating complexity: applying machine learning to improve SWL outcome prediction.
text: Shock wave lithotripsy (SWL) remains a cornerstone of non-invasive urolithiasis treatment, yet its success is highly variable and difficult to predict using traditional linear statistical models. Traditional models often fail to account for the complex, non-linear interactions between stone characteristics and procedural variables. This study aims to evaluate the efficacy of machine learning (ML) algorithms in predicting stone-free status (SFS), post-SWL renal colic, and the requirement for subsequent ureteroscopy (URS). A retrospective analysis was conducted on a multicentric database of 1498 patients treated with SWL over a six-year period. A total of 23 clinical features, including patient demographics, stone characteristics (size, density, and location), and surgical parameters, were utilized as inputs. We compared 15 different ML algorithms (including LightGBM, CatBoost, and Random Forest) and a multitask Artificial Neural Network against conventional logistic regression. Models were evaluated using validation accuracy, confusion matrices, cross-imbalance metrics (AUC-ROC, AUPRC), and F1-scores. "SFS" was defined as the primary endpoint, while secondary endpoints were represented by "Need for secondary URS" and occurrence of "Post-SWL colic". On logistic regression analysis, stone characteristics (size, density) resulted as the most important predictors of treatment failure. Treatment parameters (sessions, power) reflected procedural difficulty, and SWL success decreases with increasing stone complexity. ML models consistently outperformed traditional logistic regression across all endpoints. For the primary endpoint (SFS), LightGBM achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.83 (95% CI: 0.79-0.86) and an AUPRC of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.84-0.91). For secondary endpoints, the Need for secondary URS was predicted with high discrimination by LightGBM (AUC-ROC = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.89-0.95; AUPRC = 0.78, 95% CI: 0.71-0.84) and CatBoost (AUC-ROC = 0.89, 95% CI: 0.85-0.92; AUPRC = 0.73, 95% CI: 0.65-0.80). For Post-SWL colic (2.7% prevalence), LightGBM achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.88 (95% CI: 0.82-0.93) and an AUPRC of 0.42 (95% CI: 0.31-0.54), reflecting the realistic discrimination limits for rare post-procedural events. ML models, particularly gradient boosting algorithms, demonstrate potential in predicting outcomes after SWL. While SFS remains inherently difficult to predict due to extra-procedural factors, ML provides accurate assessments of treatment failure and complications. These tools could support more personalized clinical decision-making, helping to identify patients who may benefit from primary endoscopic intervention rather than SWL.

title: Artificial intelligence and clinical reasoning - a qualitative study with general practice trainees in Germany.
text: General practitioners face high complexity in clinical decision-making. Large language models (LLMs) may support clinical reasoning, but their impact on decision-making processes and postgraduate medical training remains unclear. This qualitative study aims to explore General Practice (GP) trainee's use of LLMs in clinical reasoning and their educational needs. GP trainees were recruited and interviewed with semi-structured interview-guide. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analysed qualitatively. Seventeen GP trainees participated (mean interview duration: 38 min; range: 21-63 min). AI was perceived as a tool to augment and accelerate clinical decision-making, while potential risks of deskilling were identified. Participants reported a lack of structured AI education and expressed a need for its integration into postgraduate training. Participants perceived AI primarily as a supportive tool that can complement clinical reasoning and improve access to medical knowledge. At the same time, they identified potential risks, including overreliance on AI-generated information and possible effects on the development of clinical expertise. These findings suggest that postgraduate medical training should address AI-related competencies, including critical appraisal, ethical responsibility and appropriate integration of AI into clinical decision-making. AI is already part of clinical practice among GP trainees, offering opportunities to support learning and clinical reasoning while raising concerns about overreliance and critical appraisal. Postgraduate medical training in GP should therefore incorporate structured AI competencies to ensure responsible, reflective and patient-centered use of AI.

title: CMR-Derived Myocardial Strain May Reflect Advanced Graft Injury Rather Than Acute Rejection After Heart Transplantation
text: AimsCardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) T1 and T2 mapping accurately detect acute heart transplant rejection, but the diagnostic value of CMR-derived strain imaging remains uncertain, particularly for right ventricular strain. Data incorporating donor-derived cell-free DNA (dd-cfDNA) into a composite reference standard are limited. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of CMR-derived left and right ventricular strain and ejection fraction for detecting acute rejection in pediatric and adult heart transplant recipients. Methods and resultsBlinded analysis of 1.5T CMR studies was performed in pediatric and adult heart transplant recipients 1-24 months post-transplant and during five additional rejection episodes 3-14 years post-transplant. Left and right ventricular strain and ejection fraction were quantified using semi-automated post-processing. Acute rejection was defined using a composite reference standard comprising endomyocardial biopsy (EMB), clinical assessment, and dd-cfDNA. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Among 214 CMR studies in 58 patients, 13 cases of acute rejection were identified. Diagnostic performance for detecting acute rejection was highest for pediatric right ventricular longitudinal strain (AUC 0.782, 95% CI 0.565-0.999), although imprecise due to data heterogeneity. All other cardiac functional parameters demonstrated limited discrimination in both pediatric and adult patients (AUC 0.536- 0.739). Models based on individual rejection indicators (EMB, clinical assessment, and dd-cfDNA) also showed poor diagnostic accuracy. ConclusionCMR-derived strain and ejection fraction showed limited diagnostic value for detecting acute rejection. Routine strain analysis therefore appears to have limited utility for rejection surveillance, with abnormalities primarily reflecting more advanced graft injury. Clinical Trial RegistrationClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04311346

title: A Local Enrichment Computational Framework to Identify Disease-Enriched Physical Activity Patterns
text: Wearable accelerometers enable continuous monitoring of physical activity (PA), yet conventional summary measures and population-wide clustering approaches may overlook disease-associated behavioral heterogeneity. Here we introduce LocPA, a computational framework that identifies disease-enriched PA patterns through confounder-adjusted activity profiling, similarity network construction, local disease-enrichment testing and community detection. Applying LocPA to 24-hour accelerometry profiles from the UK Biobank, we identified two recurring PA phenotypes across six diseases spanning cardiometabolic, neurological, psychiatric, renal and cardiovascular conditions: a low-activity phenotype characterized by reduced daytime activity and a sleep-disrupted phenotype characterized by reduced daytime and elevated nocturnal activity. In hypertension and diabetes, the sleep-disrupted phenotype was associated with greater disease burden and less favorable clinical and metabolic profiles, differences not consistently captured by conventional PA summary measures. LocPA also identified disease-specific temporal patterns, particularly in Parkinsons disease. Analyses in an independent National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey cohort supported the recurrence of hypertension- and diabetes-enriched patterns across populations and accelerometry measurements. LocPA provides a flexible, disease-driven approach for uncovering clinically relevant temporal PA patterns, with potential applications in disease risk characterization and personalized behavioral interventions.

title: Increase in Surgical Case Mix Index Across a Multi-Hospital System with Structured Limited Surgeon Chart Review
text: IntroductionHospitals face increasing financial pressures. Hospital reimbursement is tied to the Case Mix Index (CMI). The CMI is a measure of complexity of care provided by the hospital and the total reimbursement is the CMI multiplied by a base pay factor, multiplied by the total number of discharges from the hospital. The few studies in the literature have involved logistically complex attempts to improve documentation. We sought to determine whether limited, structured chart review by surgeons can improve CMI in a multihospital system. MethodsWe performed a prospective, observational study in a four-hospital academic medical system on all surgical patients from 10/2022 to 7/2026. Two clinically busy trauma surgeons performed limited structured chart reviews for select surgical patients. In the limited intervention period (1/2024-9/2024) this focused only on the trauma division. In the full intervention period (10/2024-7/2026) expanded to all surgical patients across the system. The main outcome was surgical case mix index (CMI). ResultsA total of 35,695 patients were included (13,811 pre-intervention, 9,337 limited intervention, 12,547 full intervention). CMI increased significantly among surgical patients across the whole system (2.68 (95%CI 2.65-2.71) to 2.87 (95%CI 2.82-2.92) to 2.97 (95%CI 2.93-3.01), ANOVA p <0.001). Overall length of stay was unchanged among surgical patients across the whole system. The estimated increase in revenue per patient attributable to this intervention was $3,912 in surgical patients across the system. ConclusionHaving trauma surgeons review targeted surgical patients for high value documentation capture significantly enhanced the CMI and estimated revenue of surgical services across a multi-hospital integrated health system. Such documentation reviews may represent a practical method to improve hospital documentation and revenue. Level of EvidenceLevel IV Study TypeProspective cohort study with historical controls Key MessagesWhat is already known on this topic: Documentation is critically important for hospital billing. Previous studies in trauma and acute care surgery have shown that large, intensive, and dedicated interventions can improve documentation and improve revenue generation. What this study adds: By creating a list of Major Comorbidity/Complication (MCC) and Comorbidity/Complication (CC) codes for targeted review, two clinically busy trauma surgeons were able to perform limited, targeted chart review with significant improvement in DRG capture and Case Mix Index. How this study might affect research, practice or policy: Improvements in documentation are facilitated by the targeted list of MCC and CC codes that other centers can use to improve their DRG capture, further demonstrating the financial benefit of a trauma and acute care surgery service.

title: Self-harm incidents and restrictive practice use in an acute female inpatient unit: a service evaluation of a continuous multi-system improvement approach
text: BackgroundSelf-harm is a frequent and challenging occurrence in adult inpatient psychiatric units. The use of restrictive practice to manage self-harm incidents continues to be widespread within mental health environments despite increasing national and organisational guidance to minimise its use. Purpose/aimThe aim of this project was to introduce and evaluate a continuous quality improvement programme to progressively reduce incidents of self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. The project was set in a female acute mental health inpatient unit. The project sought to embed improvements in an inpatient units interventions, procedures, and culture and staffs mindset, and move towards a sustained collaborative and positive therapeutic and communication-based approach. MethodsA retrospective service evaluation design was employed to assess differences in the number of incidents of self-harm, enhanced observation, seclusion, restraint and rapid tranquillisation in the period following the introduction of a continuous whole-systems multimodal interventional initiative in 2019. Pre- and post-initiation data were compared (2017/18 compared to 2019/2025) to evaluate improvement and whether this had been sustained. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, including frequencies, percentages, and means. ResultsSelf-harm incidents reduced between 2017/18 and 2019, with a downward trend sustained between 2019 and 2025 (136 to 72 incidents respectively between 2019 and 2025; 47% reduction). A sustained reduction in the use of restrictive practice was shown in all domains pre- and post-initiation (2017/18 compared to 2025). Clinical implicationsNo one approach will successfully reduce self-harm and the use of restrictive practice. Approaches employed have to be multi-faceted, multi-interdisciplinary, collaborative, and blend together to deliver improvement. Sustained progress requires commitment to an iterative process of continuous collaboration, improvement and adaptation.

title: Negotiating the Social Self in Chronic Spinal Pain: A Qualitative Study
text: PurposeThis study examined how people living with chronic spinal pain experience, interpret and navigate social representations of their condition and the interactions these generate across clinical, occupational, and personal settings. Materials and MethodsThirty semi-structured interviews were analysed using an approach informed by constructivist grounded theory, through initial, focused and theoretical coding. ResultsFive categories emerged, capturing how social representations and relational dynamics threatened the social self and prompted deliberate strategies for restoring agency. Theoretical coding identified a central process (maintaining and rebuilding the social self), describing how participants navigated these threats across social contexts. Notably, approximately half the participants reproduced, without revision, representations of chronic pain typical of the general population, directing judgements of simulation or inadequate effort at others with the condition. These strategies primarily aimed to restore agency and maintain a viable social self, rather than to reduce pain. ConclusionsThese findings describe one process through which social environments shape the experience of chronic spinal pain by influencing how the social self is continually negotiated. Recognising these processes may help rehabilitation professionals attend to the social dimensions of chronic pain. Implications for rehabilitationO_LIRehabilitation professionals should recognise that people living with chronic spinal pain often face a substantial and largely invisible burden beyond pain management itself. Continually demonstrating that their pain is real and legitimate can place an additional cognitive and relational burden on patients. Allowing sufficient space in clinical encounters for patients to describe these experiences may help clinicians identify the social difficulties associated with chronic pain and how they affect daily life and participation. C_LIO_LIShared experience of chronic pain should not be assumed to produce greater empathy toward others in similar situations. Approximately half the participants in this study continued to apply common social representations of chronic pain to other people with the condition. Therapeutic patient education and peer-based programmes should account for this possibility and actively address the representational frameworks participants bring to these settings. C_LIO_LIRehabilitation assessment should include patients experiences of support, disbelief, paternalism, and changing expectations across healthcare, workplace, and personal settings, as these interactions may shape perceived credibility, control and self-efficacy. C_LIO_LIClinical training in chronic pain rehabilitation should address both explicit delegitimation and more automatic forms of stereotyping, including how assumptions about what a person in pain should look like or do can influence clinical judgement and communication. C_LI

title: A Framework for Variant Filtering to Improve Diagnostic Outcomes in Genome Sequencing
text: Rare genetic disorders frequently remain undiagnosed despite the use of exome sequencing (ES) and genome sequencing (GS). This study aimed to enhance diagnostic yield by introducing a systematic framework: SMART filtering (Systematic, Multi-step, Automated, Rare variant prioritization Tool), designed to optimize GS analysis, with a particular emphasis on non-coding regions. We retrospectively analyzed 153 cases with previously negative ES and GS results. SMART filtering was applied as a pre-annotation filtering step, integrating conservation metrics, allele frequency thresholds, and splicing prediction scores. Then followed by phenotype-based prioritization and manual review. Application of this framework identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 4.6% of cases, strong variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in 1.3%, and additional candidate variants in 5.2% of cases. Several deep-intronic variants were confirmed by RNA studies and segregation analyses. The framework enabled efficient prioritization of non-coding and regulatory variants that were overlooked by standard analyses. In conclusion, SMART filtering offers a reproducible and scalable strategy to improve diagnostic yield in GS, particularly in cases where conventional analysis methods fall short. Integrating such frameworks into clinical genomic pipelines can enhance variant interpretability and diagnostic performance, ultimately leading to better patient care outcomes.

title: Pathogenic MYRF ICA Domain Variant is Aberrantly Trafficked in the RPE and Results in Isolated Nanophthalmos
text: PurposeMyelin regulatory factor is a transcription factor essential for RPE development and serves as a critical "GO" signal for eye growth. Pathogenic variants in MYRF manifest in a spectrum of clinical phenotypes ranging from isolated nanophthalmos to severe syndromic disease, in a gene dosage dependent manner. In this study, we aimed to determine the pathogenicity and molecular mechanism of a novel variant in the MYRF ICA domain, c.2083C>T (p.R695C), that leads to isolated nanophthalmos and mild retinal pigment epithelial disruption. MethodsWhole genome sequencing was performed and identified a novel MYRF variant. Pathogenecity and in silico modeling were evaluated using the Ensembl VEP tool and PyMOL. Human primary RPE and/or ARPE-19 cells were transduced with FLAG-tagged variant and wildtype MYRF or double-tagged FLAG-MYRF-MYC proteins to evaluate transcriptional activity, localization, and protein trafficking. ResultsIn silico modeling supports variant pathogenicity and altered homotrimer conformation. Functional studies in human primary RPE (hRPE) and/or ARPE-19 cells confirmed that MYRF p.R695C is cleavage deficient, mislocalized to the apical surface of polarized RPE, and demonstrated reduced synergistic transcriptional activity with co-factor SOX10 in HEK293T cells. Protein trafficking studies demonstrated that wildtype MYRF is trafficked to the apical cell surface and plasma membrane and that endogenous MYRF requires ER to Golgi trafficking pathways for proper nuclear localization and cleavage dynamics. ConclusionsTogether, these results confirm that p.R695C is pathogenic for nanophthalmos, implicate trafficking as a regulatory mechanism of MYRF in the hRPE, and support that RPE disruption as a feature of MYRF-associated nanophthalmos.

title: Accelerometer Data Harmonization and Feature Engineering for Gait Analytics
text: Gait analytics is utilized for a wide range of health-related applications, ranging from fitness tracking to medical diagnostics, and beyond. Inertial measurement units that are ubiquitously available in mobile devices provide an accessible means of gait analysis but differences in sensor specifications, placement, and recording protocols limit comparability across studies. This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and standardized quality-assessed processing pipeline to facilitate the integration and joint analysis of heterogeneous gait accelerometer data. Six publicly available datasets including a total of 935 persons were integrated into a star-schema data warehouse, and feature comparability was assessed across datasets and sensor locations. Gender classification served as a proof- of-concept downstream analysis. Gait-cycle extraction, which serves as foundation for feature extraction, was successfully achieved with an accuracy above 99% for the dataset that provides ground truth information. Comparability varied across datasets and sensor configurations, with correlation coefficients between average gait cycles ranging from 0.5 to close to 1.0. Centrally positioned sensors generally show greater correspondence than peripheral sensors, although differences in statistical features persist even between sensors at nominally identical locations. Gender classification performance remains largely near chance level, and no consistent benefit from pooling datasets could be established. These findings demonstrate that heterogeneous gait accelerometer data can be integrated and processed within a common analytical framework, but standardized processing alone does not ensure comparability of the resulting features. The proposed open-source framework implemented in Python provides a foundation for reproducible cross-study gait analysis and for investigating residual heterogeneity associated with datasets and sensor configurations. Author SummarySensors in smartphones and wearables such as smartwatches and fitness trackers enable background recording of human walking behaviour in everyday life. This data can be used in a range of health-related applications and research, both in the fitness and in the medical domain. In order to develop robust analytical methods and applications, large and diverse datasets are desirable. However, data recorded for such purposes often differ in sensor placement, hardware specification, recording procedures, and data structure, impeding the compilation of composed datasets. In this study, we develop a harmonization framework that organizes and processes accelerometer-based gait data in a standardized way. This includes a database structure, automated gait-cycle extraction, quality-control procedures, and feature-extraction methods that can be readily applied across multiple source datasets. Using six publicly available datasets, we demonstrate the technical feasibility of our approach. A subsequent downstream analysis highlights the possibilities and limits of this approach and demonstrates where differences between datasets cannot be harmonized but need to be taken into account in subsequent analyses. By providing the framework as an open-source resource, we aim to facilitate future efforts to unlock the power of large gait datasets and therewith support reproducible gait research.

title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
text: AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWClinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

title: Reducing Biosecurity Risks in Informal Poultry Slaughter: A Pilot Intervention Among Mobile Poultry Vendors in Bangladesh
text: IntroductionMobile poultry vending and slaughtering practices in Bangladesh pose potential public health risks due to poor hygiene, unsafe waste disposal, and close human-animal interactions. Limited data exist on these practices and feasible interventions to improve biosecurity among mobile poultry vendors. MethodsThis mixed-method study was conducted in three phases across four sub-districts in three districts. Phase 1 involved 416 hours of structured observation, 40 in-depth vendor interviews, and 40 informal customer interviews. Phase 2 involved the development and pilot testing of an intervention package, including poultry killing cones, hand sanitizers, disinfectants, and a hygiene pamphlet, with 10 vendors. Phase 3 implemented the intervention among 20 vendors for one month, followed by 94 hours of observation and 17 customer interviews. ResultPhase 1 found 1,959 slaughtering events with no use of personal protective equipment; slaughtering occurred in plastic jars (58%), directly on roads (21%), and roadside drains (11%). Seventy percent of vendors reported discarding slaughtering waste directly into the environment, while 78% reported not knowing how poultry diseases could spread to other animals or humans. During Phase 2, 9/10 vendors considered the killing cone useful, although bicycle users reported challenges related to weight and balance; the cone was subsequently modified. During Phase 3, 294 poultry were observed being slaughtered, with 79% using killing cones. Waste was stored in cone-attached boxes in 97% of cone uses, and vendors used hand sanitizer before eating in 75% of observed instances. Among 17 interviewed customers, 88% recognized the cones role in safer waste disposal and 53% considered it useful overall. ConclusionThis study highlights major hygiene and biosecurity gaps and demonstrates that low-cost, targeted interventions may improve biosecurity practices among mobile poultry vendors and reduce opportunities for environmental contamination in informal slaughter settings.

title: Evaluating the Quality of Diabetes Care
text: BackgroundDiabetes mellitus (DM) is an escalating global public health concern, contributing significantly to global mortalities and posing a major financial burden, particularly in Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) like Ghana [Letsa, 2023]. Suboptimal quality of care can lead to severe microvascular complications such as diabetic nephropathy (DN) and opportunistic infections like urinary tract infections (UTIs) [Letsa, 2023]. DN affects 30-40% of diabetics and is a leading cause of end-stage kidney failure, with a reported prevalence of kidney diseases of 12.5% in Ghana [Adoba et al., 2025]. Given that monitoring quality of care is crucial for prevention, this study aimed to evaluate the quality of DM care indicators, particularly focusing on urinary biomarkers, at the Ghana Ports and Harbours Authority (GPHA) hospital. MethodologyA cross-sectional design employing a retrospective medical audit was utilized, assessing patient records at the GPHA hospital Diabetes Clinic. The study population comprised 125 participants whose urinalysis data, demographics, and comorbidity categorization (Diabetes only, Diabetes and Hypertension, Diabetes and Cyesis, etc.) were collected. Urine parameters, including albuminuria, glucose, and Renal Tubular Epithelial Cells (RTEC), were retrieved from Sysmexs urinalysis analyzers (Sysmex UC 400, UF 350). ResultsThe study cohort consisted predominantly of females (58.4%, n=73) with a mean age of 54.92 years. The primary diabetic categorization was "diabetes only" (76.8%, n=96). Evaluation of albuminuria showed that mild albuminuria was recorded for only 10.4% (n=13) of participants, and overt albuminuria was absent (0.0%). This mild albuminuria prevalence is notably below the 25-30% global prevalence reported for type 2 diabetics. A significant correlation was established between the various diabetes population categories and urine glucose (Pr=0.001). Pathological RTEC results (> 2.5) were identified in three individuals, primarily from the diabetes and hypertension category (2 individuals) and the diabetes and cyesis category (1 individual). The study noted limitations, including the difficulty in acquiring the specific type of diabetes and the non-availability of data on medication type or complication level. ConclusionThe prevalence of mild albuminuria among the study population at the GPHA hospital was significantly lower than established global and certain regional Ghanaian rates. However, the detection of a significant association between diabetic categorization and glucosuria underscores the need for continuous and rigorous monitoring of renal function markers. These findings suggest that while indicators like mild albuminuria may be lower than expected in this specific cohort, targeted interventions remain essential to prevent the progression of renal complications in this high-risk population [ Adoba et al., 2025].

title: Metabolome-wide Association Study of Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia in Extremely Premature Infants
text: RationaleUntargeted metabolomics may identify novel pathways involved in bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), a poorly understood lung disease in extremely premature infants. ObjectiveTo identify metabolites and pathways altered in infants who develop BPD through a metabolome-wide association study. MethodsWe performed untargeted urinary metabolomics in 314 infants (<29 weeks gestational age) at two time points between postnatal days 5-15 and 23-32, with detailed time-series for 28 infants. We compared metabolite levels between infants with and without BPD at 36 weeks postmenstrual age using logistic regression and pathway enrichment analysis. A stratified analysis by nutrition type was performed at 23-32 days. ResultsAmong the 913 analyzed urinary metabolites, 23 and 68 were nominally associated with BPD between postnatal days 5-15 and 23-32, respectively (p<0.05). We found enrichment in the lactoyl amino acid sub-pathway (5-15 days; p=0.005, q=0.4) and xanthine metabolism and fatty acid metabolism (23-32 days; p[≤]0.002, q<0.1). Most BPD-differential metabolites were lower in infants with BPD at days 23-32 (OR=7.1, p=2x10-6), with similar patterns among infants receiving parenteral (OR=9.2, p=7x10-7) and full enteral nutrition (OR=6.1, p=0.003). Twenty-four metabolites, including vitamins C, B1, and B6, were lower in infants on parenteral nutrition with BPD at postnatal days 23-32. DiscussionBPD in extremely premature infants was associated with lower levels of vitamin-related metabolites and dysregulation of lactoyl amino acids, xanthine, and fatty acid metabolism. BPD-differential metabolites were lower in infants with BPD during the fourth week of life, potentially related to higher energy demand, metabolic dysregulation, insufficient nutrient availability, and/or impaired intestinal absorption. What is already known on this topicMetabolic dysregulation has been implicated in bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), but the metabolic pathways associated with BPD across early postnatal development remain poorly characterized. Existing metabolomic studies have been limited by small sample sizes and differences in biofluids, metabolomic approaches, and timing of sample collection, and no established metabolic biomarker exists for early diagnosis or monitoring of disease progression. What this study addsIn a large, two-cohort metabolome-wide study of extremely premature infants, BPD was associated with distinct metabolic patterns that varied by postnatal age and nutrition source, with enrichment of xanthine and fatty acid metabolism during the fourth week of life. BPD-differential metabolites were predominantly lower during the fourth week of life, particularly among infants still receiving parenteral nutrition. How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings identify metabolic and nutritional pathways for further investigation and may inform future studies of nutritional interventions aimed at reducing BPD risk in extremely premature infants.

title: The Golden Hour - Implementing and evaluating a package of interventions to improve newborn care in the first hour of life in a public sector hospital in Zimbabwe.
text: Reducing neonatal mortality remains a global priority, yet progress has stalled in many low-resource settings. Low-cost interventions such as delayed cord clamping (DCC) and early skin to skin care (ESSC) are known to reduce neonatal morbidity and mortality but implementation remains inconsistent. Prior to project initiation, Sally Mugabe Central Hospital, Zimbabwes busiest tertiary maternity unit had no documented DCC or ESSC conducted with practice limited by staffing pressures and infrastructural challenges. We aimed to implement a context-specific "Golden Hour" care bundle to improve newborn care during the first hour after birth. Using quality improvement (QI) methodology we designed interventions alongside maternity staff, including multidisciplinary training, embedded clinical support, regular feedback, leadership engagement and equipment provision. Real-time progress was tracked using the Neotree digital data tool over 12 months (November 2024-October 2025). The primary outcome was documented DCC and ESSC in eligible infants. An analysis of neonatal mortality among a subset of admitted inborn infants was also carried out. A total of 207 healthcare workers and 87 student midwives received formal training. Over 12 months, 15,292 eligible infants (81.1%) received DCC and 14,351 (76.1%) received ESSC with sustained implementation between 82-91% (DCC) and 72-85% (ESSC) for the final seven months of the project. Targeted PDSA cycles increased uptake in low birthweight infants and babies born by caesarean section. Logistic regression analysis of infants admitted to the neonatal unit demonstrated a trend to reduction in crude mortality for eligible infants receiving both interventions but this did not reach statistical significance. A multifaceted, context-specific QI programme successfully embedded evidence-based Golden Hour practices in a high-volume, resource-constrained maternity unit. Combining education, equipment, clinical support and continuous data feedback achieved sustained change in practice and a trend towards improved survival.

title: Pre- and postnatal environmental lithium exposure and adolescent neurodevelopment: a tooth-biomarker study
text: Lithium is a naturally occurring element found in drinking water, and its environmental presence is rising with demand for batteries. Yet evidence on lithium comes almost entirely from adults, ecological studies, or medical treatment, leaving the effects of prenatal and early postnatal environmental exposure unknown. We laser-mapped lithium in shed baby teeth, which preserve a record of exposure around birth (-12 to +13 weeks), from 448 U.S. youth in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study and tested associations with brain structure, cognition, and behavior at ages 9-10. Higher lithium was found in children of less-educated caregivers and from more deprived neighborhoods. Higher lithium was also linked to thicker cortices, varying surface area, mostly smaller subcortical volumes, poorer reading and language ability, and more externalizing problems, with associations varying by caregiver education. Early-life environmental lithium exposure may therefore be socioeconomically patterned and contribute to disparities in neurodevelopment, warranting environmental health surveillance.

title: SHARED GENETIC ARCHITECTURE AND DIRECTIONAL ASSOCIATIONS BETWEEN ATTENTION-DEFICIT/HYPERACTIVITY AND BORDERLINE PERSONALITY DISORDERS: AN INTEGRATIVE GENOMIC ANALYSIS
text: BackgroundAttention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and borderline personality disorder (BPD) frequently co-occur, but the contributions of shared genetic susceptibility and directional associations remain unclear. MethodsWe analyzed European-ancestry GWAS summary statistics for ADHD (38,691 cases; 186,843 controls) and BPD (12,339 cases; 1,041,717 controls). Linkage disequilibrium score regression, conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR), MR-LAP, CAUSE, colocalization, and SuSiE fine-mapping assessed genetic overlap and directional associations. ResultsADHD and BPD showed substantial genetic correlation (r_g = 0.733). ConjFDR identified 48 shared loci, of which 36 (75%) showed consistent effect directions across independent phenotype-specific comparisons. Functional annotation highlighted axon guidance, oxidative phosphorylation, and a developing midbrain cell-type signature.
